trystero: serverless WebRTC rooms for C++

trystero is a header-only port of Trystero 0.26.0’s serverless WebRTC rooms for C++20, one of the libraries of webcpp. Peers find each other over public Nostr relays and exchange messages directly, over WebRTC data channels. The wire is Trystero’s: a room joined from C++ and the same room joined from Trystero’s JavaScript are one room.

This page teaches trystero section by section: what a room is, how a program joins one in the browser and natively, how its actions carry messages, where its memory comes from, what the platform backend asks of each target, the wire it speaks, and what it guarantees. Every program it shows is one of the library’s examples, which the build compiles and links on its target. The build runs each that needs no browser over a Nostr relay of its own, and the page shows what it prints, with its twin on Trystero JS; the chat, a page, is linked and never run. The reference lists every name the headers declare.

Overview

trystero lets programs meet in a room and exchange messages directly, peer to peer, over WebRTC data channels. There is no server of the application’s own: peers find each other by publishing short signed messages on public Nostr relays, exchange the WebRTC offer and answer through them, and from then on talk over the connection the browser or the network stack established.

It ports the protocol of Trystero 0.26.0, and keeps its wire byte for byte. A room joined from C++ and the same room joined from Trystero’s JavaScript are one room: the peers see each other, and an action sent from one side arrives on the other.

The library provides:

  • room, which joins a room of an application over Nostr relays, reports the peers that join and leave, measures round trips, and leaves with Trystero’s farewell;

  • action<T>, a named channel of messages: text, JSON (webcpp::document’s), binary, or any of the three, with optional JSON metadata, of any size, sent inline or in chunks with backpressure;

  • one immutable password per app, part of every room’s sealed signaling key and challenge handshake; separate passwords use separate apps and ids;

  • every asynchronous operation as an Asio initiating function, so it completes with a callback, webcpp::asio::use_awaitable, webcpp::asio::deferred or any other completion token of webcpp::asio, which natively is Boost.Asio itself;

  • an app per program in one application and password domain, with one identity and one connection per remote peer shared by its rooms;

  • a resource for the app and an optional resource for each room, which receive their allocations (Allocation);

  • a backend interface that separates the room from the platform, and the platform backend, one implementation of it for native programs and for pages, whose WebRTC is webcpp::webrtc’s on both.

Two targets, one backend

<webcpp/trystero.hpp> is the rooms themselves, which build on both of trystero’s targets, native and emscripten, and leave the platform backend out. The backend is a header of its own, beside a page’s:

Header Target What it holds

<webcpp/trystero/platform/backend.hpp>

native and emscripten

platform::backend: webcpp::webrtc for WebRTC, natively over libdatachannel and in a page over its RTCPeerConnection and RTCDataChannel; webcpp::beast for the relays’ WebSockets, natively Boost.Beast’s and in a page its WebSocket, their URLs read with Boost.URL; webcpp::asio’s timers; and per target the sealer and the randomness, natively OpenSSL’s AES-GCM and RAND_bytes, in a page crypto.subtle and crypto.getRandomValues (The platform backend)

<webcpp/trystero/platform/page.hpp>

emscripten

platform::page_call and platform::js_string, what a page’s program uses beside the backend (In a page)

The backend runs the same room on both targets, and meets Trystero JS peers on both. Every name is in the namespace webcpp::trystero.

Requirements

  • A C++20 compiler.

  • Boost 1.92: Asio, Assert, Charconv and JSON (whose definitions webcpp::document links, its parser and its numbers), Circular Buffer, Container (its pmr base class), Endian, Hash2, System and Unordered for the rooms; URL for the platform backend’s relays, and Beast for them natively.

  • webcpp::document for every JSON text, webcpp::asio, and webcpp::webrtc and webcpp::beast for the platform backend’s WebRTC and relays (Building).

  • libsecp256k1 0.8.0, with its schnorrsig and extrakeys modules, for the BIP-340 signatures of Nostr events: every room needs it. webcpp builds it from its pinned source, /third_party//secp256k1.

  • In the browser: Emscripten 6.0.11, the version webcpp pins, a page served from a secure context (https, or http on localhost), where crypto.subtle exists, and a program whose main runs its io_context (The program runs its io_context).

  • Natively: libdatachannel 0.24.6, through webcpp::webrtc, and OpenSSL 3.

trystero raises no exception of its own: an operation that can fail completes with an error code. Every part of it, the platform backend included, compiles and works without exceptions (Exceptions).

Quick start

The quick start is one native program with two peers in it, alice and bob: each is an app of its own, with an id the program gives it, and both join the room lobby of the app webcpp-trystero-quick-start. alice greets bob when he joins, bob answers, each prints what it received, and both leave, which ends the program. In the browser the same rooms run in a page, as the chat example shows (In the browser). Running the examples builds and runs both.

Two peers in one program

An app is one peer: its id among the peers, its relays and its STUN servers. The program gives each app its id, app_config::self_id, where an app would draw 20 random characters, so that what it prints is the same on every run. It meets over the relay whose URL is in the environment, TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL, which the lane relayed starts on 127.0.0.1, and then keeps its peers on the machine; without it, the program uses Trystero’s public relays and STUN servers, as every program that names none does:

#include <webcpp/trystero.hpp>
#include <webcpp/trystero/platform/backend.hpp>

#include <boost/asio/as_tuple.hpp>
#include <boost/asio/awaitable.hpp>
#include <boost/asio/co_spawn.hpp>
#include <boost/asio/detached.hpp>
#include <boost/asio/io_context.hpp>
#include <boost/asio/use_awaitable.hpp>

#include <chrono>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

namespace asio = boost::asio;
namespace trystero = webcpp::trystero;

/** What one peer's app is made with: its id, and the relay `relay` names, or the public ones. */
trystero::app_config config_for(std::string_view self_id, const char* relay) {
    trystero::app_config config;
    config.app_id = "webcpp-trystero-quick-start";
    // An id of the program's own, where an app would draw 20 random characters, so that what each
    // peer prints of the other is the same on every run.
    config.self_id = self_id;
    if (relay != nullptr) {
        // The peers stay on this machine: the relay given, and a STUN server where nothing answers
        // in place of Trystero's public ones, beside a backend bound to the loopback.
        config.relay_urls = {relay};
        config.ice_servers = {{.urls = {"stun:127.0.0.1:9"}, .username = {}, .credential = {}}};
    }
    // Without a relay, both lists stay empty: Trystero's defaults, as a user's program has them,
    // the public relays its app id selects and Trystero's public STUN servers.
    // A connection closes as soon as no room uses it, so that the program ends once both leave.
    config.idle_timeout = std::chrono::milliseconds{0};
    return config;
}

main makes one platform::backend for both apps, joins each app to the room, and makes in each room the action chat, whose messages are std::string. alice greets each peer that joins, once its handshake completes, with a message to that peer alone, and prints what she receives, after its sender’s id, then leaves. bob’s part is a coroutine. run returns once no work is left: each room closes its relays as it leaves, and each connection closes as soon as no room uses it:

int main() {
    // The relay the lane starts on 127.0.0.1, or none: Trystero's public relays.
    const char* const relay = std::getenv("TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL");
    asio::io_context io;
    // One backend for both apps, whose connections stay on the loopback beside a local relay.
    trystero::platform::backend_config local;
    if (relay != nullptr) {
        local.bind_address = "127.0.0.1";
    }
    trystero::platform::backend backend(io.get_executor(), local);

    // Two apps, two peers, each with its own id, in the same room.
    trystero::app alice(io.get_executor(), backend, config_for("alice", relay));
    trystero::app bob(io.get_executor(), backend, config_for("bob", relay));
    auto alice_lobby = alice.join("lobby");
    auto bob_lobby = bob.join("lobby");
    if (!alice_lobby || !bob_lobby) {
        std::cerr << "not joined\n";
        return 1;
    }
    auto alice_chat = alice_lobby->make_action<std::string>("chat");
    auto bob_chat = bob_lobby->make_action<std::string>("chat");

    // alice greets each peer once its handshake completes, prints the answer, and leaves.
    alice_lobby->on_peer_join([&](std::string_view peer) {
        alice_chat.async_send("hello", {.targets = {trystero::peer_id(peer)}, .metadata = {}},
                              [](boost::system::error_code ec) {
                                  if (ec) {
                                      std::cerr << "not delivered: " << ec.message() << '\n';
                                  }
                              });
    });
    alice_chat.on_message([&](const std::string& text, const trystero::message_info& info) {
        std::cout << info.from << ": " << text << '\n';
        alice_lobby->async_leave([](boost::system::error_code) {});
    });
    asio::co_spawn(io, answer(*bob_lobby, bob_chat), asio::detached);

    io.run();  // lint-run: the program's network I/O; libdatachannel's threads post to it
}

bob awaits the first message with async_receive, prints it after its sender’s id, answers its sender with async_send, and leaves with async_leave. asio::as_tuple hands each error over as a value, so a room left first ends the wait instead of throwing:

/** bob's part: waits for a message, prints it, answers its sender, and leaves the room. */
asio::awaitable<void> answer(trystero::room& lobby, trystero::action<std::string>& chat) {
    // as_tuple hands the error over as a value: a room left first ends the wait without throwing.
    auto [ec, text, info] = co_await chat.async_receive(asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
    if (ec) {
        co_return;
    }
    std::cout << info.from << ": " << text << '\n';
    auto [failed] = co_await chat.async_send("hello back", {.targets = {info.from}, .metadata = {}},
                                             asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
    if (failed) {
        std::cerr << "not delivered: " << failed.message() << '\n';
    }
    co_await lobby.async_leave(asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
}

The program prints bob’s line, then alice’s:

alice: hello
bob: hello back

Its twin on Trystero JS prints the same two lines. Trystero draws one selfId per page, so bob is a second page there, and each peer prints the other’s name where the C++ program prints the id it gave the app:

import {joinRoom} from 'trystero'
import {RTCPeerConnection} from 'werift'
import {openPage} from '../page.mjs'

// Trystero draws one selfId per page, so bob is another page, and each peer prints the other's
// name where the C++ program prints the ids it gave its apps. The peers meet on this machine
// alone: no ICE server, werift's WebRTC for Node.
const config = {
    appId: 'webcpp-trystero-quick-start',
    relayConfig: {urls: [process.env.TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL]},
    rtcConfig: {iceServers: []},
}

// bob's part: waits for a message, posts the line the twin prints for it, answers its sender, and
// leaves the room.
const bob = openPage(async ({joinRoom, RTCPeerConnection, data, post}) => {
    const room = joinRoom({...data, rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}, 'lobby')
    const chat = room.makeAction('chat')
    const [text, {peerId}] = await new Promise(received => {
        chat.onMessage = (...message) => received(message)
    })
    post(`alice: ${text}`)
    await chat.send('hello back', {target: peerId})
    await room.leave()
}, config)

// alice greets each peer that joins, prints the answer, and leaves.
const room = joinRoom({...config, rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}, 'lobby')
const chat = room.makeAction('chat')
room.onPeerJoin = peerId => chat.send('hello', {target: peerId})
const answer = new Promise(received => {
    chat.onMessage = text => received(text)
})
console.log(await bob.next())
console.log(`bob: ${await answer}`)
await Promise.all([room.leave(), bob.done])

In the browser

In a page the same app and room are C++ compiled to WebAssembly, over the page’s own WebSocket and RTCPeerConnection. The chat example keeps what a page’s program keeps for as long as the page lives: an io_context, the platform::backend on its executor, the app, the room joined through it, and its actions:

struct chat {
    webcpp::asio::io_context io;
    trystero::platform::backend backend{io.get_executor()};
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::app> app;  // made at the first join, with that join's app id
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::room> room;
    // The action "chat" twice: received as views of the frame, and sent by moving the text.
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::action<std::string_view>> messages;
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::action<std::string>> outgoing;
};

A page and its program shows how it joins, sends, and runs its io_context from main, and Running the examples serves it. Two tabs of the chat that join the same app and room meet; so do a native peer and a page, which the lane interop proves with Trystero JS pages in headless Chrome (The oracle and the interop lanes).

Building

trystero is header-only, and is developed inside the webcpp superproject, as a Boost library is developed inside Boost. It builds on three libraries of webcpp’s: webcpp::asio; webcpp::webrtc, the platform backend’s WebRTC; and webcpp::beast, its relays’ WebSockets, on both targets. Its native TLS and WebRTC dependencies, and libsecp256k1, are built from pinned sources:

Library Needed by Found where

libsecp256k1 0.8.0, with its schnorrsig and extrakeys modules

every room: it signs the Nostr events peers meet through

/third_party//secp256k1, built from third_party/libs/secp256k1

webcpp::asio

every room

/webcpp/asio//asio: natively Boost.Asio, on emscripten the backend it ships

webcpp::webrtc

the platform backend’s WebRTC, on both targets

/webcpp/webrtc//webrtc, the superproject’s libs/webrtc

webcpp::beast

the platform backend’s relays: their WebSockets, and natively their TLS

/webcpp/beast//tls natively, Boost.Beast over the source-built OpenSSL; /webcpp/beast//browser in a page, over the page’s WebSocket

Boost.URL

the platform backend’s relays: their URLs, on both targets

/webcpp//boost_url, built from Boost’s sources once per variant

libdatachannel 0.24.6

the platform backend natively, through webcpp::webrtc

/webcpp/third_party//libdatachannel, built from third_party/libs/libdatachannel

OpenSSL 3.5.9

the platform backend natively: its WebRTC, its relays’ TLS, its sealer and its randomness

/webcpp/third_party//openssl, shared by the Asio, Beast and Trystero build graphs

The tables of libsecp256k1 are chosen by the feature webcpp-secp256k1-tables. With auto, the default, natively they are window 15 and comb 11x6: a larger program, and faster signing and verification. On emscripten they are window 2 and comb 2x5: the same signing, verification a little slower than window 4, and a smaller program. A program that wants otherwise asks for <webcpp-secp256k1-tables>small or <webcpp-secp256k1-tables>large.

In a b2 project

A program uses trystero through /webcpp/trystero//platform, the rooms and the platform backend (The platform backend), on either target: natively, built with threading=multi, and in a page. /webcpp/trystero//trystero is the rooms alone, which adds trystero’s headers, Boost’s, webcpp::asio, libsecp256k1 and webcpp::document with Boost.JSON’s and Boost.Charconv’s definitions, compiled once per variant, and no WebRTC on any target: a program that runs its rooms over a backend of its own, as trystero’s tests run whole rooms over the memory relays (Testing a program that uses trystero), needs no more:

alias parts : :
  : : <include>include <library>/boost//headers <library>/webcpp/document//document
  <library>/webcpp/config//config <library>/webcpp/asio//asio <library>/third_party//secp256k1 ;
alias trystero : : : : <library>parts
  <toolset>emscripten,<webcpp-suspend>asyncify:<linkflags>"-sASYNCIFY_REMOVE=@\"$(WEBCPP_TRYSTERO_ROOT)/asyncify-remove.json\""
  ;

/webcpp/trystero//trystero is parts, which brings those dependencies, and, under Asyncify, the list that leaves Boost.JSON’s recursive descent out of Asyncify’s instrumentation (JSON texts). A program of a part that parses no JSON, as trystero’s tests of the timer, a relay’s URL, a page’s calls and the sealer are, links parts, or platform-parts (below), in place of the rooms: it has none of the parser’s functions, and Binaryen warns of a pattern of the list that names none.

On emscripten webcpp::asio builds without threads, since the page has none, links embind, and links its runtime in the suspension variant the build asks, webcpp-suspend=jspi by default or asyncify; a program is named after it, as the chat’s chat-program-60-d-jspi.js. embind is linked as a flag, -lembind, rather than with b2’s own <embind>on: that feature is not free, and b2 ignores a feature that is not free among usage requirements, so a program that used it would not link.

/webcpp/trystero//platform adds the platform backend to the rooms: platform-parts, the backend over parts, with an alternative for each target, which trystero’s tests of the backend’s parts that parse no JSON link alone. Natively it adds webcpp::webrtc, with libdatachannel and the same source-built OpenSSL used by Asio and Beast; webcpp::beast’s TLS over that OpenSSL for the relays’ WebSockets, /webcpp/beast//tls; Boost.URL, which reads the relays’ URLs; and webcpp::asio’s //tls, whose make_tls_client_context() gives a program webcpp’s embedded authorities in place of the system’s, which the backend trusts by default (The relays). In a page it adds webcpp::webrtc, over the page’s own RTCPeerConnection; webcpp::beast’s //browser, over the page’s WebSocket; and Boost.URL, which reads the relays’ URLs there too. A page links no OpenSSL:

alias platform-parts : : <toolset>emscripten
  : : <library>parts <library>/webcpp/webrtc//webrtc
  <library>/webcpp/beast//browser <library>/webcpp//boost_url ;
alias platform-parts : : <conditional>@platform-dependencies
  : : <library>parts <library>/webcpp/webrtc//webrtc
  <library>/webcpp/beast//tls <library>/webcpp/asio//tls
  <library>/webcpp//boost_url ;
alias platform : : : : <library>platform-parts <library>trystero ;

Natively the platform backend’s WebRTC, libdatachannel’s, uses worker threads, so each consumer declares <threading>multi. Its OpenSSL dependency is the matching threaded variant; a single-threaded native program that uses the backend is rejected before compilation, with an error that says to add <threading>multi. A page has no threads, and needs none.

The platform backend works with exceptions and without them (Exceptions), so a program builds as it asks, as the examples do, the quick start natively with <threading>multi, which the build runs over a relay of its own (Running the examples):

webcpp.drive quick_start : quick_start.cpp
  : <library>/webcpp/trystero//platform <threading>multi : run_over_relay.mjs : : native ;

and as trystero’s own tests of the platform backend do, on each target that builds them, once without exceptions too, a test of a part that parses no JSON over platform-parts ($(platform-part)):

webcpp.run platform_backend : platform_backend_test.cpp : $(platform) ;
webcpp.run platform_sealer : platform_sealer_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <testing.input-file>fixtures/expected/expected.json ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket_unreachable : platform_websocket_unreachable_test.cpp
  : $(platform) ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket_url : platform_websocket_url_test.cpp : $(platform-part) ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket : platform_websocket_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <define>_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_EXTENSIVE
    <define>_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS
  : native ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket_allocation : platform_websocket_allocation_test.cpp
  : $(platform) : native ;
webcpp.run platform_peer_connection : platform_peer_connection_test.cpp
  : $(platform) : native ;
webcpp.run platform_room : platform_room_test.cpp : $(platform) : native ;
webcpp.run platform_backend_no_exceptions : platform_backend_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <exception-handling>off ;
webcpp.run platform_sealer_no_exceptions : platform_sealer_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <testing.input-file>fixtures/expected/expected.json <exception-handling>off ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket_unreachable_no_exceptions : platform_websocket_unreachable_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <exception-handling>off ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket_url_no_exceptions : platform_websocket_url_test.cpp
  : $(platform-part) <exception-handling>off ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket_allocation_no_exceptions : platform_websocket_allocation_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <exception-handling>off : native ;
webcpp.run platform_peer_connection_no_exceptions : platform_peer_connection_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <exception-handling>off : native ;
webcpp.run platform_room_no_exceptions : platform_room_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <exception-handling>off : native ;

A page’s program is linked for the web, with a memory that grows, as the chat’s is:

webcpp.link chat : chat.cpp
  : <linkflags>-sENVIRONMENT=web <linkflags>-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH : emscripten ;

The emscripten toolset

The emscripten target is b2’s emscripten toolset, registered against Emscripten 6.0.11 from emsdk, as a user-config.jam declares it, where $(emsdk) is the emsdk’s directory and $(node) the node that runs a program:

local emsdk = /path/to/emsdk ;
local node = /path/to/node ;
using emscripten : : $(emsdk)/upstream/emscripten/em++ : <nodejs>$(node) ;

With it and the pinned source submodules initialized, from the root of a webcpp checkout, these build the tests and the examples, natively and on emscripten:

b2 libs/trystero/test libs/trystero/example
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/trystero/test libs/trystero/example

Preparing the dependencies

Initialize the native dependencies from the superproject root:

git submodule update --init --recursive third_party/libs/openssl third_party/libs/libdatachannel \
  third_party/libs/secp256k1

Install CMake 3.21 or newer, Perl and Make (native Windows Perl and nmake with MSVC). B2 builds OpenSSL, libdatachannel and its pinned nested libjuice, usrsctp and libsrtp sources for the configured compiler, standard library, runtime and build variant. Upstream sources are verified and copied to a disposable build directory; the checkout is never patched. The resulting headers and separate static archives stay in B2’s variant directory, and the final link contains exactly one OpenSSL archive pair.

libdatachannel’s own WebSocket, examples and tests are disabled; media transport remains enabled. System OpenSSL and installed libdatachannel binaries are never fallback providers. A combined Asio/Beast/Trystero application uses the same native <threading>multi configuration for all three libraries.

Running the examples

The quick start and the programs of the appendix "Differences" (Differences from Trystero) run natively in the lane relayed, each over a Nostr relay of its own on 127.0.0.1, which example/run_over_relay.mjs starts and names to the program in TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL: a program passes when it ends by itself having printed its .expected. Node runs the relay, with the packages test/oracle pins. The first command runs the lane, the second the quick start alone:

b2 libs/trystero/example//relayed
b2 libs/trystero/example//quick_start

The quick start’s executable stays under the build directory. Run without TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL, it meets over Trystero’s public relays and STUN servers, as a program that names none does, and prints the same two lines (Two peers in one program) within seconds, then ends:

`find bin/libs/trystero/example/quick_start.test -name quick_start -type f`

The chat needs a browser, so the build links its program and never runs it (A page and its program). The target site copies the page and its program into a directory of its own under the build directory, out of the tree, and prints it. The page is served from localhost, where crypto.subtle exists:

b2 toolset=emscripten libs/trystero/example/chat//site
python3 -m http.server 8000 -d `find bin/libs/trystero/example/chat -name site -type d`

At http://localhost:8000, two tabs that join the same app and room, the page’s webcpp-trystero-chat and lobby unless their user changes them, meet over the public relays within seconds: each counts the other as a peer, and what one sends appears in the other. On another toolset, site stops the build, saying that the page is built on emscripten alone.

Rooms and actions

A room is what Trystero’s joinRoom returns, and an action what its makeAction returns: this section is the C++ form of both.

Joining

An app is this program in one application and password domain: one peer id, one immutable password, and one connection to each remote peer, which every room of the app it shares with that peer uses, as a Trystero JS page shares them. Constructing it takes the executor every handler and completion runs on, the backend, which must outlive it, and its configuration, app_config, moved. A room is joined with join, which returns a boost::system::result<room> to test, or an error: error::already_joined while a room of that id is joined in the app, and error::too_many_rooms when 64 rooms count, since a peer drops a connection that advertises more. Joining an id in its 99 ms farewell finishes that farewell first and joins afresh.

join and the app’s other methods run where its executor runs. An app and all its rooms use that executor; a multithreaded io_context needs a strand. Destroying or moving over the app handle releases it; its rooms keep the app’s state alive and continue. Two app objects, even with the same app id, are two peers. Rooms with different passwords use separate apps with distinct self ids. A room has no password override; changing the domain password requires a new app. No registry or identity is kept in static storage.

app_config member What it is

app_id

The application’s id, Trystero’s appId: rooms of different apps never meet.

self_id

One id for every room of the app; empty, 20 random characters drawn once. An id longer than 64 bytes is replaced and reported. This id links the app’s rooms: rooms that must not be linked to one program use an app each (What remains).

password

The immutable password shared by every room of this app, copied into the app’s resource. It contributes to each room’s sealed signaling key and challenge handshake. Empty, the app is passwordless. Different passwords require separate apps and distinct self ids; they share no connections, presence or tokens (What remains).

relay_urls

The Nostr relays. Empty, relay_redundancy of Trystero’s 29 defaults, shuffled with the app id so every peer picks the same ones. Their configuration is the app’s; sockets and the Nostr signing key remain per room.

relay_redundancy

The number of default relays to use, 5.

ice_servers

The STUN and TURN servers; empty, default_ice_servers(). An unusable URL, or a TURN server without a user name and credential, is dropped and reported to app::on_error with error::invalid_configuration.

idle_timeout

How long a connection with no rooms stays after a departure, 123,333 ms; 0 closes it immediately. A negative value becomes 0 and is reported. A connection whose last binding was kicked closes at once.

log

One sink for the app and its rooms, called with a category (app, nostr, signal, webrtc, room or action) and a sentence composed in the app’s resource. Empty, no text is composed.

memory

The app’s resource, std::pmr::get_default_resource() by default; it must be non-null (Allocation).

app_config is move-only because its log sink is a handler: pass it moved, or build it in place. Each room adds room_options:

room_options member What it is

handshake_timeout

How long a binding has to finish the handshake, 10 s.

max_receive_bytes

The most bytes the room reserves for incoming transfers across peers, 256 MiB.

max_json_document_bytes

The largest image a received JSON payload’s document may take of the room’s resource, webcpp::document’s default, 64 MiB; a payload past it is not delivered (JSON texts).

memory

The room’s own resource; null uses the app’s resource.

Peers

on_peer_join and on_peer_leave set what is called with each peer whose handshake completed, and with each joined peer that leaves; peers() lists the joined peers. on_error sets what is called with each problem with one peer that the room handled itself, as Trystero’s onPeerError: a peer with signals under another password, a malformed room proof, a handshake that timed out, a connection the backend refused. It is called with an empty peer id for a count of signals that did not open with the room key (Bounded signaling). Each handler replaces the one set before, and every view it receives is valid for the call.

async_ping measures the round trip to a joined peer, from sending @_ping to receiving its @_pong.

async_leave says goodbye to every peer, Trystero’s @_leave, gives the farewell 99 ms, as Trystero waits, then detaches its bindings and closes its relay sockets, and every pending operation completes with error::room_left. Destroying a room leaves at once, without the 99 ms, and so does assigning another room over a joined one: every peer is told, and every pending operation completes with error::room_left, even while an action of it lives.

A kick or a peer’s @_leave ends only that room’s binding: the app’s other rooms keep using the connection. When it stays live, rebinding waits one step after the end, initially the larger of handshake_timeout and 10 s, plus 1 s, doubling after each further end to at most 5 minutes. A completed handshake or the connection’s end resets the count. After its own kick the lower id refuses bindings until that time and keeps frames; the higher id drops frames until it sends presence, but accepts the lower id’s presence. A binding also requires the peer to have advertised the token itself, by its presence or by a frame of the room on its connection. A peer on a protected app’s shared connection already authenticated with that app’s password through the initial sealed negotiation. A peer that knows it can still send a wrong room proof: only the lower id reports that proof as wrong_password; the higher id answers and sees a departure. Malformed challenge data is rejected by its receiver too. This room handshake retains Trystero JS 0.26.0’s one-way wire behavior.

Actions

An action is a named channel of messages, wire compatible with Trystero’s makeAction. Its name has 1 to 32 UTF-8 bytes and no NUL; with another, every send fails with error::invalid_action_name. Its type says how messages travel and how they are received:

Type Trystero format Received as

std::string

text

a copy of the bytes

std::pmr::string

text

a copy of the bytes, in the room’s resource

std::string_view

text

a view of the frame it arrived in, valid during the handler

webcpp::document::document

JSON

parsed into a document of its own, with the standard allocator

webcpp::document::pmr::document

JSON

parsed into a document of the room’s resource, which holds its image and the parse’s working state

trystero::bytes

binary

a copy of the bytes

trystero::pmr_bytes

binary

the transfer’s buffer, moved when resources match, otherwise copied once into the room’s resource

std::span<const std::uint8_t>

binary

a view of the frame, valid during the handler

trystero::payload

any

a std::variant of std::string, webcpp::document::document and bytes, by format

A JSON payload is webcpp::document’s: a webcpp::document::document the program builds or parses, with the standard allocator, or a webcpp::document::pmr::document, whose image a memory resource holds, the room’s when it is received; the pair mirrors std::string and std::pmr::string. A C++ peer sends the bytes JSON.stringify writes of the same value, which Trystero JS sends, for every value JavaScript can hold: its strings, booleans and nulls, its keys in JavaScript’s order, array indices first, and every number a double holds, written as JavaScript writes it. A number a double cannot hold, an integer past 253 or a decimal of more digits, is sent exact, as webcpp::document holds it: a Trystero JS peer reads the nearest double, or Infinity past a double’s range. A text that does not parse is not delivered, nor one nested deeper than 256 or holding a lone surrogate, which JSON.parse takes, nor one whose document passes the room’s room_options::max_json_document_bytes, 64 MiB of image by default, some 350,000 values of one character, which a program lowers to bound what a peer’s JSON may take of its room’s resource (JSON texts).

A document is moved, never copied: so payload, which may hold one, has no copy assignment, and in a build without exceptions no copy constructor either; nor has a document a default constructor there, where a program makes one with create() or webcpp::document::parse, each of which returns a result, given the resource’s allocator for a webcpp::document::pmr::document. A handle of a document’s values refers to the document object, as every handle of webcpp::document does: moving the document invalidates it, so a handler that keeps a received document moves it and reads it through the handles of the document it moved it into. A webcpp::document::pmr::document move-assigned to one of another resource copies its image into that resource, and raises std::bad_alloc through boost::throw_exception when the resource has no room: a program without exceptions keeps one by move construction, std::optional::emplace for one. The room test sends one:

if (auto negroni = webcpp::document::parse(R"({"drink":"negroni"})")) {
    a.make_action<webcpp::document::document>("drink").async_send(
        std::move(*negroni), [&](boost::system::error_code ec) { sent.push_back(ec); });
}

receives it:

drink_z.on_message(
    [&](webcpp::document::document v, const trystero::message_info&) { drink = std::move(v); });

and reads it:

BOOST_TEST_EQ((*drink)["drink"].value_or(std::string_view()), "negroni");

A message of another format than the action’s type is not delivered to it. Several actions of different types may share a name: one receives as views, another sends by moving strings, as the chat does (A page and its program).

Messages arrive at the handler on_message sets, with a message_info: the sender’s id and the metadata it passed. Without a handler they queue, up to 1024 per action, the oldest dropped first, for async_receive, which needs an owning type: a view would outlive the message; a message of another format, or a JSON text that does not parse, completes it with error::transfer_rejected and an empty value, which allocates nothing: an empty container, in the room’s resource for a std::pmr type, and for a JSON one webcpp::document’s nothing(), a document with no image whose root reads undefined. Frames of an action that arrived before it was made are kept, 64 per peer for 120 s, and delivered to it once it is.

async_send sends to send_options::targets, or to every joined peer, with optional JSON metadata. A payload that fits one 16 KiB frame with its header and metadata travels inline; a larger one is offered, accepted by the receiver within 120 s, and sent in chunks of at most 16,370 bytes. A frame or a chunk is handed to the data channel only while the channel buffers at most 64 KiB, waiting at most 10 s for it to drain. async_send completes once each target’s local data channel has taken the inline frame, or the last chunk of the transfer the receiver accepted, with the first failure if any, as Trystero’s send resolves: nothing confirms that the receiver has the message. A receiver takes one transfer per peer at a time, accepts it only for an action with a receiver, and reserves at most max_receive_bytes across peers.

Completion tokens and ownership

Every asynchronous operation is an Asio initiating function. With a callback it calls it on the room’s executor; with webcpp::asio::use_awaitable it resumes a coroutine; with webcpp::asio::deferred it returns an operation started later. webcpp::asio is Boost.Asio itself natively, so Boost.Asio’s tokens are the same there; on emscripten they are webcpp::asio’s.

Because a deferred operation starts after the call, the arguments of an asynchronous operation are owned: async_send takes its value by value, moved when the type owns its storage, copied once at the call into the room’s resource when it is a view, and written at once, into the room’s resource, when it is a JSON document; send_options owns its strings; and async_ping copies the peer id at the call. Everything else that only reads text takes a std::string_view.

Errors

Operations complete with a boost::system::error_code in the category webcpp.trystero, of the enumeration error:

Value Meaning

room_left

the room was left while the operation was pending

no_such_peer

the target is not a joined peer

peer_disconnected

the peer went away before the operation finished

invalid_action_name

an action’s name is not 1 to 32 UTF-8 bytes without NUL

metadata_too_large

the metadata does not fit one frame

transfer_rejected

the receiver refused the transfer, or a message had another format than the awaited type

transfer_timed_out

the receiver neither accepted nor refused within 120 s

channel_stalled

the data channel stopped draining for 10 s

wrong_password

a peer’s signals or handshake used another password, or a handshake message had the wrong shape

handshake_timed_out

a connected peer did not finish the handshake in time

handshake_failed

reserved: nothing reports it today

backend_failure

the browser or the native stack refused an operation

invalid_configuration

the app dropped an unusable configuration value and continues without it

already_joined

a room of that id is already joined in the app

too_many_rooms

the app already holds 64 rooms, including farewells

Allocation

A webcpp library lets its user choose where its allocations come from. trystero does it through std::pmr, header-only, with an app resource, an optional resource for each room, and a resource for the platform backend’s own state.

The app’s resource, the room’s and the backend’s

  • app_config::memory, std::pmr::get_default_resource() by default, receives the app’s state, configuration copy including its password, self id, registry, shared connections, advertised tokens, kept frames, drain order and presence frames. Peer connections, data channels and received frames use it even while a room negotiates them. The logger, sink and every sentence of the app and its rooms use this resource too. It must be non-null, checked by BOOST_ASSERT at app construction.

  • room_options::memory, the app’s resource when null, receives the room’s state, bindings and their drain waiters, negotiation records, rebinding counts and backoffs, sealed texts, relays, actions, queues, outgoing frames, transfers, the documents of the JSON texts it reads, and handlers. The signing context is made there with secp256k1_context_preallocated_create.

  • platform::backend_config::memory, std::pmr::get_default_resource() by default, receives the platform backend’s own state: its copy of bind_address, its window of constructions and its own webcpp::webrtc runtime. It must be non-null, and outlive the backend and every connection of its runtime. What the backend makes for an app or a room is in the resource given with that call instead (Asio, the backends, webcpp::document and the protocol).

  • Adoption replaces negotiation handlers with the app’s; ending a negotiation clears the room’s handlers. Detachment fails and frees a binding’s drain waiters and removes its registrations before returning. After a room ends, the app retains no allocation in that room’s resource.

  • A received frame starts in the app’s resource. A pmr_bytes payload moves from its message buffer when that buffer and the room use the same resource; otherwise it is copied once into the room’s resource. A chunked transfer assembles its buffer in the room’s resource. Received std::pmr::string text is always copied once into the room’s resource. A JSON text is parsed into a webcpp::document::pmr::document of the room’s resource, a remote candidate into one of the app’s, and a JSON payload received as a webcpp::document::pmr::document into one of the room’s resource: the document’s image, which holds every value, strings included, and the working state of the parse that made it.

All resource access runs on the app’s executor. A resource need not be thread-safe when that executor runs on one thread; several io_context threads require a strand.

The allocation test builds every part of app_config in its counted resource before the counting window, including strings, relay URLs, ICE servers and log sink; app_config_in and options_in name both resources:

/** An app's configuration, every part of it in `memory`, made before the window. */
trystero::app_config app_config_in(counting_resource& memory, std::string_view self_id,
                                   std::string_view relay, std::size_t& lines) {
    return trystero::app_config{
        .app_id = std::pmr::string("allocation", &memory),
        .self_id = std::pmr::string(self_id, &memory),
        .password = std::pmr::string("a password", &memory),
        .relay_urls =
            std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string>({std::pmr::string(relay, &memory)}, &memory),
        .ice_servers = std::pmr::vector<trystero::backend::ice_server>(&memory),
        .log =
            {
                std::allocator_arg,
                std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>(&memory),
                [&lines](std::string_view /*category*/, std::string_view /*text*/) { ++lines; },
            },
        .memory = &memory,
    };
}

/** A room's options, naming `memory` explicitly. */
trystero::room_options options_in(counting_resource& memory) {
    return trystero::room_options{.memory = &memory};
}

How long the resource lives

The app’s resource must outlive its state: the app handle, every room of it, retained values allocated there and every pending operation. A room’s own resource must outlive that room, its retained std::pmr::string, pmr_bytes and webcpp::document::pmr::document values, and its pending operations. The backend’s resource must outlive the backend and every connection of its own runtime, which a handler the io_context still holds may keep alive. Destroying a handle closes its work but queued completions can still free memory. Declare the backend_config::memory, app_config::memory and room_options::memory resources before the io_context, then construct the backend, app and rooms. Drain or destroy the io_context before destroying any of these resources. In the browser, keep them until all pending promises settle: a pending async_await holds its handler, so in practice resources live for the page’s life.

No check in debug builds catches the misuse: trystero holds a raw pointer and cannot see the resource end, and the use comes after the room is gone, from an operation of Asio’s or of the browser’s. A resource that asserts nothing is out when it is destroyed, as the test’s counting resources do, is the check, and it is the user’s.

A room allocates and frees on every event, a frame, a parsed text, a post or a log line, so a resource that reuses what is freed, a pool such as std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource, suits a long-lived room; a std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource grows with every event and suits a short-lived one, or a test.

Completion handlers

A completion handler is the user’s, and is allocated as its own associated allocator says: the room never binds its allocator over it. webcpp::asio::bind_allocator gives one the room’s resource. The allocation test makes the allocator of a resource:

const auto in = [](counting_resource& memory) {
    return std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>(&memory);
};

and binds it over the completions of a transfer and of a ping, so that they too are allocated in the sender’s resource:

a.make_action<trystero::pmr_bytes>("file").async_send(
    trystero::pmr_bytes(100'000, 7, &a_memory),
    webcpp::asio::bind_allocator(in(a_memory),
                                 [](boost::system::error_code /*ec*/) {}));
a.async_ping(z.self_id(),
             webcpp::asio::bind_allocator(
                 in(a_memory),
                 [&pings](boost::system::error_code ec,
                          std::chrono::milliseconds /*rtt*/) { pings += ec ? 0 : 1; }));

When the room erases a completion handler’s type (an any_completion_handler), it records whether the handler’s associated executor is the room’s, which only the concrete type tells without allocating; such a completion runs from an operation the room posts to its executor, allocated with the handler’s allocator. One bound to another executor is handed to that executor by Asio, whose type-erased executor wraps it with std::allocator.

Containers and shared objects

Every container trystero declares is a std::pmr one or a Boost container over std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator: std::pmr::string (and peer_id), std::pmr::vector (and backend::bytes, protocol::bytes and pmr_bytes), std::pmr::deque, std::pmr::map and std::pmr::set, and boost::unordered_flat_set (the event ids a strategy remembers), boost::circular_buffer (the construction window, the recent challenges) and boost::circular_buffer_space_optimized (the replay cache), built over their owner’s resource; app_config, room_options, send_options, message_info and backend::ice_server hold them too. Two types stay the user’s choice of std::allocator: trystero::bytes, a std::vector<std::uint8_t>, and trystero::payload, a variant of std::string, webcpp::document::document and bytes. A received bytes, or the binary of a payload, is a copy of the frame, which starts in the app’s resource; a received webcpp::document::document is in the standard allocator, its image and the working state of its parse, as document’s document is. webcpp::document::pmr::document is document’s own allocator-aware type, over std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<std::byte>, which receives in the room’s resource.

A struct that holds std::pmr containers takes the room’s std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<> in its constructor, and a container of such structs is given it when it makes one, with try_emplace(key, allocator). A std::pmr container is never copied without an allocator: its copy constructor takes the default resource, so a copy names the resource, std::pmr::string(text, allocator). Moving keeps the resource.

Shared objects are made with std::allocate_shared over std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>, never with std::make_shared, std::make_unique or new; a timer is a std::shared_ptr for that reason.

No type of trystero is a data structure meant for a shared segment, one that a process builds there and another maps and uses in place: every type is a run-time object, an app, a room, an action, a socket, a handler or the backend, routed through the std::pmr resources above, or a value one takes or gives. A std::pmr container holds its resource and its storage at absolute addresses of its process, as a handler holds a callable, so none is shareable in the sense of Boost.Interprocess, and none takes an Allocator template parameter for it.

Handlers

std::function takes no allocator since C++17, so trystero holds every handler it keeps in handler<R(Args...)>, a move-only callable that allocates through a std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>. Constructed with handler(std::allocator_arg, allocator, f), it holds f inline when f fits in three pointers and is nothrow-movable, and in storage of the allocator otherwise. It replaces every std::function of the backend interface (the handlers of its timer, WebSocket, data channel, peer connection and sealer), of the room and of the log’s sink. Constructed from f alone it uses the default resource; the app moves app_config::log into its resource with the allocator-extended move. A move assignment carries the source’s allocator with its target.

Asio, the backends, webcpp::document and the protocol

Asio, webcpp::asio’s, which natively is Boost.Asio itself. Every post, dispatch, timer wait and any_completion_handler the room makes carries webcpp::asio::bind_allocator over its resource. A post through webcpp::asio::any_io_executor is wrapped by Asio in a function object allocated with std::allocator, from Asio’s per-thread recycling cache, which calls std::aligned_alloc on a miss (measured: two per post, in every round of five posts, natively and on emscripten). So the room, and the platform backend’s sealer, post through the executor of an io_context when the executor they were given is one, where Asio allocates the operation as the handler’s allocator says, and in a page the sealer awaits each Web Crypto promise through it too, so that its settlement is posted the same way. On another executor, a strand over the io_context for one, the wrapper stays Asio’s (What stays outside the resource). The executor is the program’s: the examples and the tests give the app and the backend the executor of their io_context.

The backends. Each method of backend::factory that makes an object takes a std::pmr::memory_resource* as its last parameter. Peer connections, data channels and received frames use the app’s resource; relay sockets, sealers and room timers use the room’s. Objects and their handlers allocate through that supplied resource. The backend’s WebRTC (The backend’s WebRTC) gives webcpp::webrtc’s connections and channels a std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator on the app’s resource, which their state, their queues, their texts and their operations use: each operation’s handler is bound to it. The platform backend’s relays are one session of webcpp::beast’s on both targets, made in the room’s resource with its handlers, its queued texts and its read buffer, and each of its operations’ handlers carries the room’s allocator, so that what Asio and Beast allocate for them is there too. Natively Boost.Beast’s stream state stays Beast’s (What stays outside the resource); in a page the WebSocket stream’s own state is in the room’s resource too, since the stream is made with std::allocator_arg and the room’s allocator. The platform backend’s own state, its copy of bind_address, its window of constructions and its own runtime, is in backend_config::memory (The app’s resource, the room’s and the backend’s): the test platform_backend, on both targets, makes a backend while a counting resource is the default one, which sees none of it, and sees backend_config::memory given all of it back once the backend is destroyed.

webcpp::document is allocator-aware: a webcpp::document::pmr::document allocates through a std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<std::byte> its image, one buffer in which Boost.Interprocess’s rbtree_best_fit heap holds every value, strings included, with offsets for pointers, and the working state of what reads or writes it: the parser’s state, the path and the pending key and text of the value being read, the tree’s record of each change, and the writer’s stack, each freed before the call that made it returns. trystero reads each text with webcpp::document::parse(text, options, allocator) into a document of the room’s resource, of the app’s for a remote candidate: its image starts at 4 KiB and grows in place, twice as large each time, up to twice the caller’s bound and 64 KiB for a protocol text, and for a JSON payload up to 96 times its length and 64 KiB, which every valid payload fits, or the room’s room_options::max_json_document_bytes, 64 MiB by default, the smaller: the most a peer’s payload takes of the room’s resource. A text given whole leaves Boost.JSON’s parser no state to suspend. A text the room writes is appended field by field to a std::pmr::string of its resource, its strings quoted by webcpp::document::quote, which allocates only through that string, and a JSON payload is written by webcpp::document::stringify_to in pieces of 8 bytes, which no standard library’s string keeps outside its own object, its writer’s stack in the document’s own allocator.

The protocol (protocol/) takes a std::pmr::memory_resource* as the last parameter of every function that returns what it allocates, with the default resource as its default, and returns std::pmr types. protocol::nostr::verify uses secp256k1_context_static and allocates nothing.

What stays outside the resource

  • libdatachannel’s and OpenSSL’s own allocations, the copy libdatachannel’s C API makes of a message before webcpp::webrtc reads it into the frame, and, natively, webcpp::webrtc’s copies of what libdatachannel’s threads report, in the standard allocator;

  • what emscripten::val holds, in the JavaScript heap;

  • Asio’s own once-per-context allocations: its services, in a page webcpp::asio’s bridge among them, and the scheduler’s first operation;

  • the wrapper Asio puts around a post through an executor that is not the executor of an io_context, a strand for one, and, given such an executor, around the settlement of each Web Crypto promise of a page’s sealer;

  • webcpp::webrtc’s posts from libdatachannel’s threads, which carry Asio’s default allocator, since the resource is touched only on the room’s executor; and the wrapper Asio puts around webcpp::webrtc’s completions, which it posts through webcpp::asio::any_io_executor;

  • natively, for each relay connection, what Boost.Beast and Asio allocate of their own, which takes no allocator from a handler: the state of the WebSocket stream and of the TCP stream under it, the WebSocket’s write buffer, made at its first write, and, over TLS, the two 17 KiB buffers of Asio’s TLS stream; the resolver’s state and its results, with what the C library’s getaddrinfo allocates on Asio’s resolver thread; the WebSocket handshake’s request and response and the header fields of both, the response’s header at most 8 KiB, which webcpp::beast’s bounded handshake layer reads through Beast’s own parser, reading no byte of the body of a response that refuses the upgrade (before it, Beast read such a body up to its default 8 MiB: an 8 MiB body held about 18 MiB at its peak), and keeping a header line split between two reads in the room’s resource; over TLS, the verify callback Asio’s set_verify_callback makes with new, with the copy of the host that host_name_verification holds, a std::string; each wait of Beast’s timers, from Asio’s per-thread recycling cache, which calls std::aligned_alloc on a miss: the TCP stream’s deadline over the connection and the TLS handshake, and the WebSocket’s handshake, idle and close timeouts, the idle one started again at each read, so a wait of a message’s; and each keep-alive ping’s frame, with new. The WebSocket’s operations, its read buffer and its queued texts are in the room’s resource on both targets, since each of its handlers carries the room’s allocator, and natively a message allocates nothing else outside it: operator new sees none from the send of a text to the receipt of its echo (the test platform_websocket_allocation). The reads’ and the writes’ completions are a handler of the session’s own, with no executor of its own: Asio’s any_completion_handler, whose executor is of another type than the stream’s, had Asio make an any_completion_executor with new for each operation and wrap each completion in a function object of its recycling cache (measured: six operator new and four of its blocks for a text sent and its echo received);

  • in a page, for each event of a relay’s WebSocket, its open, each message and its close, the C library’s allocation embind makes for the std::string into which webcpp::beast’s page stream reads the event’s type (event["type"].as<std::string>() in its deliver), and for a message a second, for the type of its data (data.typeOf().as<std::string>() in its receive_message), each freed before the call that made it returns: two for each message a relay sends. The test platform_page_relay_allocation counts exactly these, no more and no fewer, from a connection’s call to its open, for one message and for ten, and from its close to the page’s close event. The stream’s own state, its operations, the messages it holds and the read buffer are in the room’s resource, and the page’s WebSocket makes the handshake; webcpp::asio’s page resolver holds its results, the host and the service, in place, and allocates nothing, whatever the host’s length. Embind’s strings stay: they are freed at once, and avoiding them would need webcpp::beast’s page stream to read an event’s type without a std::string;

  • the payload types std::string, bytes, webcpp::document::document and payload, with std::allocator, the user’s choice;

  • on Emscripten, the C library’s select(), which Asio’s reactor calls on every wait of an io_context with a timer or a socket, and which callocs an array on every call;

  • on Emscripten under Asyncify, the unwind data Asyncify allocates whenever the browser program’s run suspends;

  • in the browser, the storage of the map in which webcpp::asio’s bridge finds each pending Web Crypto promise, in the allocator of the io_context, made for the first and grown when more are pending at once than it holds, and kept until the io_context is destroyed. The rest of a page’s seal or open, the wait for its promise and the post of its settlement, is in the room’s resource when the backend’s executor is that of an io_context: the test platform_page_sealer_allocation, after a first seal and open, sees neither operator new nor the C library allocate from the start of a seal or an open to its completion. The registrations of a WebSocket and of a page_call are intrusive, the events of a socket are posted in the room’s resource, and the calls of a page_call in the resource it is given.

The test’s memory relays are shared by every room of a test: they allocate their relays through the resource they are constructed with.

The proof

test/allocation_test.cpp, on both targets, counts the global operator new, which it replaces, and the C library’s allocation functions, where the platform lets a program see them: glibc’s are replaced and forward to __libc_*, Emscripten’s dlmalloc has weak definitions the test replaces, and macOS reports each to malloc_logger; MSVC’s are not counted, nor any under AddressSanitizer, whose own allocator reports to none of these. Only the thread main runs on is counted, and every global allocation it counts is kept, by its address, in a table of a fixed size until it is freed.

  • Two rooms over the memory relays exchange a payload, a std::pmr::string, a pmr_bytes and a webcpp::document::pmr::document in turn, the document written by the sender and parsed by the receiver: neither operator new nor the C library sees an allocation, none is out when the window closes, and the counting resources of the two configurations see the rooms’. The same exchange, with a handler that allocates outside the resources, an operator new it leaves out until the window closes and a call of the C library, sees exactly those: the zeros are not for want of counting.

  • Each text a room reads, a relay’s event carrying an offer, a relay’s OK, a signal, a handshake message and a candidate, is parsed into a document of a counting resource: neither operator new nor the C library sees an allocation, and the image goes back to the resource with the document.

  • Two rooms with a password, a log sink and the relays’ state in a resource of its own are made, join, exchange a payload that travels in chunks, measure a round trip, one says goodbye, both are destroyed and the io_context is drained. From the first construction to the drain, while the rooms and the relay read and write their JSON texts, neither operator new nor the C library sees an allocation. Once the rooms are destroyed their resources still have memory out, the operations they left pending, and none once the io_context has drained.

  • Two apps with two rooms each exchange binary payloads, one room using the app’s resource and one its own. Size-specific counters prove one payload copy into the distinct room resource, and no extra copy when resources match. From construction through the drain neither operator new nor the C library sees an allocation, and every resource ends with nothing out.

The counting resources also count a return of memory they never gave, a std::pmr object freed through the wrong resource, which must be none. Asio’s once-per-context allocations are made before anything is counted; without them, the 6 they make would still be out at the drain. On Emscripten the test also replaces select() with one that keeps its array on the stack, so that the count sees the rooms’ allocations rather than the C library’s wait; and, under Asyncify, where the test’s own run_for suspends, it marks Asyncify’s allocation of a suspension’s unwind data and counts it apart, as webcpp::asio’s allocation test does. The test runs in both of webcpp::asio’s suspension variants. It is declared in test/Jamfile:

webcpp.run allocation : allocation_test.cpp : <toolset>emscripten:<linkflags>-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH ;

The platform backend

platform::backend implements the backend interface on both targets, one class for a native program and for a page (<webcpp/trystero/platform/backend.hpp>, /webcpp/trystero//platform). Its WebRTC is webcpp::webrtc’s, natively libdatachannel's and in a page the page’s own RTCPeerConnection and RTCDataChannel (The backend’s WebRTC); its relays’ WebSockets are webcpp::beast’s, natively Boost.Beast’s own and in a page its WebSocket; its timers are webcpp::asio’s steady_timer. Two parts are the target’s own, chosen by WEBCPP_TARGET_EMSCRIPTEN: the sealer, natively OpenSSL’s AES-GCM and in a page crypto.subtle, and the source of randomness, natively OpenSSL’s generator and in a page crypto.getRandomValues, called from JavaScript that catches what it throws. Its clocks are the standard library’s on both: std::chrono::system_clock for Nostr’s created_at, and std::chrono::steady_clock for its timing, which Emscripten reads from the page’s Date.now() and performance.now().

A room over it is the same room as a browser’s or Trystero JS’s: they meet over the same relays and exchange the same frames. One backend serves every app and room of the program, with separate app objects and distinct self ids for different passwords, beside the executor it runs on, and the program runs that executor’s io_context itself: natively blocking on it or polling it (Two peers in one program), in a page from main, as webcpp::asio’s model has it (The program runs its io_context).

Its configuration

platform::backend_config is what the backend makes its peer connections, its relays and its own state with, beside the app’s ice_servers:

Member What it is

bind_address

The local address every peer connection binds to, as "127.0.0.1"; empty means every interface but the loopback. Bound to the loopback, the peers of one machine connect with no other network, which a test wants; a peer bound there reaches no other machine. Natively only: a page’s RTCPeerConnection cannot bind, and webcpp::webrtc refuses every connection a page asks it to bind, so a page leaves it empty.

max_peer_connections_per_minute

The most peer connections the backend makes in any minute, for every room in every app it serves together, 256: beyond, it makes none, and a room reports each negotiation it cannot start. A room makes at most 64 in any 57 s however its peers behave (Bounded signaling), so the default lets four rooms do so at once. A connection still counts against its negotiating room’s 57 s window after adoption by the app; presence and reuse make none.

runtime

What the backend’s own webcpp::webrtc runtime is made with, webcpp::webrtc::runtime_options: its max_peer_connections, the most connections alive at once, 256 by default, beyond which the backend makes none and a room reports each negotiation it cannot start; and, natively, thread_pool_size, libdatachannel’s threads, its own default when 0. Unused when the backend is given the program’s runtime (The runtime).

relay_limits

What the relays’ WebSockets tolerate of a relay that stops reading or answering, platform::websocket_limits (The relays).

memory

The resource of the backend’s own state, the default resource unless the program gives one: its copy of bind_address, its window of constructions and its own runtime. It must not be null, and must outlive the backend and every connection of its runtime. What the backend makes for an app or a room is in the resource given with that call instead (Allocation).

The runtime

webcpp::webrtc’s runtime caps the peer connections alive at once, and, natively, holds what libdatachannel keeps for the whole process, its threads and its global state. A backend makes one of its own, with backend_config::runtime, or takes the program’s: platform::backend(ex, runtime, config), or platform::backend(ex, tls, runtime, config) with the program’s TLS context too (The relays). Each of its connections and channels keeps that runtime alive, so that one which outlives the backend, in a handler the io_context still holds, never outlives the runtime. A connection gives its place back once it is gone.

Natively a process holds one runtime at a time, since libdatachannel’s state is the process’s: a program with several backends at once, or that uses webcpp::webrtc beside trystero, makes one webcpp::webrtc::runtime before its io_context and gives it to each.

In a page the cap counts every RTCPeerConnection of the page, every program and runtime of it together, from its construction until the garbage collector frees it, as Chromium counts them against its own 500 (measured with headless Chrome: the 501st throws "Cannot create so many PeerConnections", and a closed one counts until a collection): webcpp::webrtc’s census of the page counts every connection it makes, with any runtime. The default, 256, is half of Chromium’s, so that a closed connection still counts until a collection the page cannot ask for, while the rest of Chromium’s count stays free for what the page makes without a room.

The relays

The relays are reached over webcpp::beast, on both targets with the same session: natively over Boost.Beast’s own WebSocket, in a page over its WebSocket; ws:// in the clear, wss:// over TLS. Each connection is a chain of Asio operations on the room’s executor (resolve, connect, TLS, the handshake, then one read after another, and one write at a time), whose handlers carry the room’s allocator, so that what Asio and Beast allocate for them, the read buffer among it, is in the room’s resource (Allocation); the reads’ and the writes’ handlers have no executor of their own, so that Asio wraps none of their completions. In a page the stream’s own state is there too. What stays outside it is listed in What stays outside the resource: natively, for each connection, what Beast, Asio and OpenSSL allocate of their own, which takes no allocator (their streams’ state, the resolver’s, the handshake’s request and response, the verify callback, their timers’ waits and each keep-alive ping’s frame), and a message allocates nothing more than the wait of the idle timer, from Asio’s per-thread cache; in a page, for each event of the page’s WebSocket, the string embind makes of its type, two for a message. A write that fails ends the connection, which reports its close at once. A relay’s messages are texts (NIP-01): a binary one is dropped, on both targets. The WebSockets are Beast’s rather than libdatachannel’s own, so the relays run on the room’s executor like everything else.

A relay’s URL is read with Boost.URL, on both targets, by the same rules. It accepts ws:// and wss://, the scheme in any case; a host name, with its escapes decoded, in lower case; an IPv4 address as a dotted quad (ws://127.0.0.1:7447/), also with escaped digits, which is then an address and not a name; an IPv6 address in brackets (ws://[2001:db8::1]:7447/), whose address without them is what the resolver looks up, and which the handshake names as it is written; and a port up to 65535, the scheme’s when the URL names none. It refuses a URL of another scheme, http:// and https:// among them, which a page’s WebSocket alone would take as ws:// and wss://; one without a host, with userinfo or with a fragment; an IPvFuture address (ws://[v1.x]/); and a host with a byte that a page’s URL parser refuses in a host, escaped or not: a space or a control character, or one of #, %, /, :, <, >, ?, @, [, \, ], ^ and |.

It fails closed on what a page’s URL parser accepts but reads otherwise: an IPv4 address in another form than a dotted quad, which a page reads as the address and the system’s resolver might reach under another name, as the shorthand 127.1, octal or hexadecimal parts (0x7f.0.0.1), a final dot or a single number, and so any host whose last label is a number, which a page reads as an address or refuses; an international domain name, which a page turns into its A-label (xn--bcher-kva.example for bücher.example) and this parser does not, with its bytes beyond ASCII escaped or not; a tab, a newline or a backslash anywhere in the URL, which a page drops or reads as a slash; and a character that RFC 3986 allows in no path, as a space, { or a byte beyond ASCII, which a page escapes and Boost.URL refuses. A refused URL makes the relay report a close, as an unreachable one does, and the room retries it later as it would any other.

Over TLS the connection asks for the relay’s verification on both targets, whatever the verify mode of the context: it sets verify_peer on its stream. A program’s context made as Asio makes a client’s, ssl::context(ssl::context::tls_client), whose verify mode is verify_none, still has every relay verified; the context itself is left as it is. Natively the connection names the relay’s host to the server (SNI) when it is a name, never when it is an address, verifies the relay’s certificate against the context’s authorities, and checks it against the URL’s host, a name or an address, with a verify callback of its own: of the context, its authorities, its client certificate, its options and its protocol versions hold, and its verify mode and verify callback do not. In a page the browser does all three, against its own authorities, and webcpp::beast’s page stream refuses a context that asks for what a page cannot honour: authorities added, a client certificate or key, options, a method other than tls_client or sslv23_client, or a verify callback other than host_name_verification of the relay’s host. Such a context makes no WebSocket, and every wss:// relay reports a close. By default the backend makes its TLS context with platform::make_tls_context(): natively TLS 1.2 or newer, and the system’s certificate authorities, those OpenSSL’s default verify paths name; in a page a context that records only the policy the page’s stream asks for, a client that verifies its peer. A relay whose certificate does not verify is unreachable, and the room retries it later.

On Windows OpenSSL’s default verify paths are a cert.pem file and a certs directory in its build-time directory, SSL under the common program files (C:\Program Files\Common Files\SSL on a usual machine), which neither Windows nor webcpp fills, and OpenSSL reads no Windows certificate store by default: there the system’s authorities are none unless SSL_CERT_FILE or SSL_CERT_DIR names some. make_tls_context() succeeds there all the same, and no wss:// relay verifies, so a Windows program gives the backend its own context, webcpp’s embedded roots as below.

A native application that trusts other authorities makes its context and gives it to the backend: webcpp’s embedded Mozilla roots, which read no file of the system, with webcpp::asio::make_tls_client_context(), or a private authority with webcpp::asio::make_tls_client_context(pem):

trystero::platform::backend backend(io.get_executor(), webcpp::asio::make_tls_client_context());

The backend takes the context as make_tls_client_context returns it, a boost::system::result: one that holds an error, as when OpenSSL cannot make the backend’s own, is kept, tls_context() returns it, and every wss:// relay reports a close while the ws:// ones are still reached. No constructor throws. tls_context() also gives the context itself, which an application may configure further before the backend connects to a relay, natively; in a page what it adds that the page cannot honour, as above, has every wss:// relay report a close.

A relay is a third party, and the backend bounds what one can make the room hold:

  • A text longer than 1 MiB (protocol::max_relay_message_bytes) closes the connection before it is copied, in a page before it enters WebAssembly, the relay’s first texts too: the bound is set before the handshake, since a page can deliver a relay’s first messages in the same task as its open.

  • A relay that stops reading is dropped once the text held unsent for it would pass 4 MiB (websocket_limits::max_queued_bytes, which is protocol::max_queued_relay_bytes): the session’s own queue, and in a page also what its WebSocket holds unsent, its bufferedAmount, which webcpp::beast’s queue_limits::send bounds to the same.

  • In a page, the texts a relay sent that wait for the room’s executor are bounded too, at webcpp::beast’s queue_limits::receive, 4 MiB: past it the socket closes.

  • Natively, a relay that answers the handshake with a status other than 101 has its response’s header read, at most 8 KiB, and no byte of its body, and the connection reports its close; the room retries with its backoff. Beast’s WebSocket stream reads the response with a parser of its own, inside its handshake, whose limits none of its options reaches, so the session’s next layer is webcpp::beast’s bounded handshake layer (websocket::bounded_handshake_stream, with response_limits::body 0), which reads the response through Beast’s parser within those bounds and hands the handshake no more: a relay’s refusal with a body of 4 MiB made the room’s thread allocate 4,199,353 bytes before it, and 5,144 now, the connection’s own state among them (platform_websocket_allocation). In a page the browser makes the handshake.

  • Natively, a relay that stops answering is dropped once idle_timeout (30 s) passes with its keep-alive ping unanswered: halfway through, the connection sends a ping. The timeout counts bytes received, and a ping waits for the write in flight, so a relay that reads under about 2 KB/s is closed during a 64 KiB text. Signaling texts are 2 to 4 KB, so a real room meets it only with a relay slower than about 200 B/s. A page’s WebSocket cannot ping, and webcpp::beast’s page stream refuses keep-alive pings, so a page has no idle timeout.

Each drop reports one close, and the room reconnects with its backoff (Discovery over Nostr).

Randomness and sealing

The backend’s randomness, the room’s keys and nonces, and the IV of each seal come from the platform’s one secure source, its result checked: OpenSSL’s RAND_bytes natively, and in a page crypto.getRandomValues, at most 65536 bytes a call, which the backend calls from JavaScript that catches what it throws: a page whose getRandomValues is missing or throws has no randomness, and no JavaScript exception enters WebAssembly, where Emscripten’s getentropy let it through. When it has none, random() aborts the program, since nothing is safe without it, and a seal fails with error::backend_failure.

The sealer is asynchronous on both targets, as Web Crypto is: natively it works synchronously and posts its completion, and in a page it awaits each Web Crypto promise with webcpp::asio’s browser::async_await, under a key it imports on its first operation, while the operations that arrive meanwhile wait with a copy of their text. A completion never runs inside the call that started it. A settlement that is not an ArrayBuffer, which only a page whose crypto.subtle was replaced gives, fails the seal or the open with error::backend_failure.

Exceptions

trystero raises no exception of its own, and the platform backend works with exceptions and without them on both targets, as the rest of trystero does. Natively libdatachannel reports errors by throwing, but webcpp::webrtc calls its C API, which catches what it throws and returns a code: a refused description, candidate or channel completes with error::backend_failure, a connection the platform refuses is not made, and no exception crosses into trystero. In a page no JavaScript exception enters WebAssembly (No JavaScript exception enters WebAssembly).

<webcpp/trystero/config.hpp>, which every header includes first, defines WEBCPP_TRYSTERO_NO_EXCEPTIONS when webcpp has no exceptions (WEBCPP_HAS_EXCEPTIONS is not defined: the compiler has none, or the program defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS); a developer may define it for trystero alone in a build that has them. It changes nothing in trystero’s behaviour. No function of the backend throws, its constructors included: when OpenSSL cannot make the relays’ TLS context, the backend keeps the error as a value, which tls_context() returns, and every wss:// relay reports a close, as an unreachable one does (The relays).

Natively

Threads

libdatachannel delivers its events on threads of its own. Neither webcpp::webrtc nor the backend runs a handler there: webcpp::webrtc posts each event to the room’s executor, through a weak reference, so an event that arrives after its object is gone does nothing. Every handler of the room and every completion runs on the executor, as in a page. An application that runs the io_context on several threads gives the app a strand, shared by all its rooms. A native program that uses the backend is built with threading=multi (Building).

If a transport closes during adoption, before the room obtains a binding, the room forgets that negotiation and restarts announcements. Its later close event cannot leave signaling marked connected with no binding.

What the backend asks of libdatachannel

What libdatachannel does is webcpp::webrtc’s: its C API, which works without exceptions, automatic negotiation off, so that an offer or an answer exists only when the signaling asks for one, as in a page, and every object it hands out held until its owner lets it go. The backend adds:

  • Its connections bind to backend_config::bind_address.

  • A TURN URL with a user name and a credential is written turn:user:credential@host, the form libdatachannel parses (webcpp::webrtc’s ice_server).

  • A URL libdatachannel cannot parse, as a stuns: one, a scheme it does not know, is left out of the connection, each URL being tried alone, where a page’s RTCPeerConnection refuses the whole connection.
