  • What libdatachannel allocates inside itself is libdatachannel’s (What stays outside the resource).

In a page

In a page the backend is given the executor of the program’s io_context, which the program runs from main. One backend serves every app and room of the page. Apps with different passwords use distinct self ids and share no connection or presence. <webcpp/trystero/platform/page.hpp>, which builds only on emscripten, holds what a page’s program uses beside it: platform::page_call and platform::js_string.

The program runs its io_context

A page’s program is the shape of any program of webcpp::asio: main makes the io_context, the backend, the app and its rooms, and calls io.run(), which runs the rooms’ handlers on the stack of main and suspends into the browser’s event loop whenever nothing is ready (webcpp::asio’s run family, in either suspension variant).

  • The page’s events reach C++ through webcpp::asio’s bridge, a service of the io_context: a socket’s open, message or close, a settled Web Crypto promise, and webcpp::webrtc’s events are each posted to the io_context, and run when the run family resumes, never inside the event.

  • The backend’s timers are webcpp::asio’s steady_timer, in the reactor’s timer queue: they fire while the program runs its io_context.

  • The program holds a work guard on the io_context for the page’s life: a page that waits for its user, or for its peers, has no work of its own, and without the guard run would return.

  • The page reaches C++ through platform::page_call, a function of webcpp::asio’s bridge that the program hands to the page, and whose every call only posts its work to the io_context. Nothing calls run, poll or dispatch from a JavaScript event: while run is suspended, an event sees the io_context as running in this thread, and a call of the run family there fails at its first suspension (webcpp::asio’s guide, "Who may call it"). Nor is a page’s call an embind function: under Asyncify, while the run of main is suspended, an embind function returns a promise that never settles, and its second call aborts a debug build (measured with Emscripten 6.0.11).

  • The handler of a page_call is a handler of the run, and lets no JavaScript error out, webcpp::asio’s rule for every handler, which its guide gives where it says what a JavaScript error out of a handler does: an error that leaves it leaves run with it, and the program’s run never resumes (measured with Emscripten 6.0.11 under node: the process ends with the error, in either suspension variant). A page may pass any value, so the handler checks its type before it converts it, with isString(), isNumber() or typeOf(), and reads a field only of what is neither null nor undefined: embind’s as<std::string>() of a number throws a BindingError, and a field of undefined a TypeError. The handler is given the page’s value as it is when the handler runs, not when the page called: a JavaScript object the page changes meanwhile is seen changed.

  • A page_call posts each call in the resource it is given, which holds the call until the io_context runs it or is destroyed: the resource outlives the io_context. A call through a function the page kept after its page_call was destroyed, or after the io_context was, reaches nothing, and a page_call destroyed after its io_context is harmless.

So nothing runs while nothing happens, a handler runs as soon as the run family resumes after its event, and a turn of max_handlers_per_turn handlers is followed by a yield, which lets the page render. A handler’s C++ exception propagates out of run to main, as it does natively.

How JavaScript reaches C++

Every function the page calls with an event, or with a call of its own (platform::page_call), is made by webcpp::asio’s bridge, for a registration and a key that is never reused, and only posts to the io_context: an object registers when it is made and removes its registration when it is destroyed, so a late event for a destroyed object finds nothing. The relays’ sockets are webcpp::beast’s, whose page stream also scopes each event to its connection, so that an event of a socket already dropped reaches nothing. A Web Crypto promise is awaited with webcpp::asio’s browser::async_await, whose settlement is posted the same way and whose operation is outstanding work until it settles. webcpp::webrtc’s objects receive the page’s WebRTC events through the same bridge. Their JavaScript is linked into every program on emscripten by /webcpp/asio//asio: a program includes no source file of trystero’s.

Text that crosses into JavaScript is decoded straight from the WebAssembly memory a view points into, platform::js_string, and text that comes back is encoded straight into storage of the object’s resource: no std::string is made to carry either.

No JavaScript exception enters WebAssembly

The backend makes every call into JavaScript that can throw, a WebSocket constructor or send, a Web Crypto method, crypto.getRandomValues, in JavaScript that catches what it throws: webcpp::beast’s page stream turns a socket that cannot be made into an error, and its relay reports its close; a Web Crypto call is made inside an async function, so that what it throws becomes the rejection of its promise, which the C++ turns into the error its interface has, and its settlement is read only when it is an ArrayBuffer; and crypto.getRandomValues, missing or throwing, is a platform without randomness (Randomness and sealing). webcpp::webrtc’s JavaScript catches the page’s WebRTC exceptions the same way. The bridge’s functions catch what still escapes a delivery, put WebAssembly’s stack pointer back and report it, and with exceptions a C++ exception is caught in C++, which frees it. So a page’s program may be built with exceptions or without them, and a peer’s malformed message never stops it.

What a page bounds

  • A data channel message is read by webcpp::webrtc, a text as the UTF-8 it holds and a binary one as its bytes, and dropped on the executor when it is a text, as a peer can send, or larger than any room frame (protocol::max_room_frame_bytes): neither can be a frame. webcpp::webrtc bounds what it reads: a message past max_message_size (256 KiB), or unread messages past max_received_bytes (16 MiB), close the channel.

  • A relay’s texts are bounded as natively, the first ones it sends in the task of its open too, and its socket’s bufferedAmount and its texts waiting for the executor too (The relays); a binary message is dropped; a page has no idle timeout.

  • A page makes at most runtime_options::max_peer_connections (256) peer connections across all apps and rooms it serves, counted from their construction until the garbage collector frees them (The runtime), and at most backend_config::max_peer_connections_per_minute (256) in any minute, as natively. Beyond, the rooms report each negotiation they cannot start.

Peer connections, data channels and received frames use the app’s resource; relay sockets, their events, timers and sealed signaling texts use the room’s. Presence or reuse binds another room without making another peer connection.

What a page needs

  • A secure context: https, or http on localhost or 127.0.0.1. Elsewhere crypto.subtle, which seals the signaling, does not exist, and every sealing operation fails with error::backend_failure.

  • No threads: Emscripten’s threads need a cross-origin isolated page, so trystero uses none. Its Asio is webcpp::asio’s, built without threads when the program has no pthread ABI, and main runs it on the page’s one thread.

  • A suspension variant of webcpp::asio, which /webcpp/trystero//platform brings: webcpp-suspend=jspi, the default, for a browser with JavaScript Promise Integration, or asyncify for any other. The run of main suspends in either, and a page loads a variant its browser runs: the chat’s site is built in one, JSPI unless the build asks for webcpp-suspend=asyncify (Running the examples).

  • Under Asyncify, no more of its stack than webcpp::asio’s 8,192 bytes (webcpp::asio’s guide, "Asyncify’s stack"). A room’s work runs in handlers, between the run’s waits, so that when run suspends the stack holds the frames of main and of webcpp::asio alone. In a debug build, the deepest, the chat’s two pages, which joined one room over the public relays, met over WebRTC and exchanged a message, suspended at most 1,032 bytes deep, the interop test’s page in its 26 scenarios at most 920, and the tests of a page’s program at most 1,600; in a release build, linked at -O3, 328, 348 and 384 (measured on 2026-11-15, Emscripten 6.0.11). A program that runs the io_context from deep in its own code, under large frames, measures its own suspensions and asks for more with asyncify-stack-size, as webcpp::asio’s guide says; trystero’s tests run each case in a frame of its own instead (How trystero is tested).

  • A program that runs its io_context from main for as long as the page lives, under a work guard: the io_context must outlive every room and object it serves, and its handlers run only while it runs.

  • webcpp::document, with Boost.JSON’s and Boost.Charconv’s definitions, and Boost.URL’s definitions, which a program links from /webcpp/document//document and /webcpp//boost_url, which /webcpp/trystero//platform brings and which build on emscripten as on every target.

A page and its program

The chat example is a page whose room is C++: the program joins and sends, and the page only draws. It keeps the io_context, the backend and the room for the page’s life, and makes the action chat twice: once as std::string_view, to receive a message as a view of its frame, and once as std::string, to send by moving the text:

struct chat {
    webcpp::asio::io_context io;
    trystero::platform::backend backend{io.get_executor()};
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::app> app;  // made at the first join, with that join's app id
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::room> room;
    // The action "chat" twice: received as views of the frame, and sent by moving the text.
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::action<std::string_view>> messages;
    std::unique_ptr<trystero::action<std::string>> outgoing;
};

The program joins the app and the room its user typed, and sets its handlers; it reads the page’s form only once it knows it holds two strings, since its handler lets no JavaScript error out (The program runs its io_context), and a received message goes from its frame straight into a JavaScript string:

void join_room(chat& c, const val& form) {
    // The page's value is checked before it is read: a page_call's handler lets no JavaScript
    // error out of the run, which reading a field of null or undefined (a TypeError) or converting
    // what is not a string (embind's BindingError) would.
    if (c.room || form.isNull() || form.isUndefined()) {
        return;
    }
    const val app_field = form["app"];
    const val room_field = form["room"];
    if (!app_field.isString() || !room_field.isString()) {
        return;
    }
    const auto room_id = room_field.as<std::string>();
    if (!c.app) {
        trystero::app_config config;
        config.app_id = app_field.as<std::string>();
        config.log = [](std::string_view category, std::string_view text) {
            ui("log", category, text);
        };
        c.app = std::make_unique<trystero::app>(c.io.get_executor(), c.backend, std::move(config));
    }
    auto joined = c.app->join(room_id);
    if (!joined) {
        ui("log", std::string_view("chat"),
           std::string_view("not joined: " + joined.error().message()));
        return;
    }
    c.room = std::make_unique<trystero::room>(std::move(*joined));
    c.messages = std::make_unique<trystero::action<std::string_view>>(
        c.room->make_action<std::string_view>("chat"));
    c.outgoing =
        std::make_unique<trystero::action<std::string>>(c.room->make_action<std::string>("chat"));
    c.room->on_peer_join([](std::string_view peer) { ui("peerJoined", peer); });
    c.room->on_peer_leave([](std::string_view peer) { ui("peerLeft", peer); });
    // A view of the received frame: the text goes from the frame straight into a JavaScript string.
    c.messages->on_message([](std::string_view text, const trystero::message_info& info) {
        ui("message", std::string_view(info.from), text, false);
    });
    ui("joined", c.room->self_id(), std::string_view(room_id));
}

send_message ignores a value that is not a string, shows the message at once, and reports a failure in the page’s log:

void send_message(chat& c, const val& message) {
    if (!c.room || !message.isString()) {
        return;
    }
    auto text = message.as<std::string>();
    if (text.empty()) {
        return;
    }
    ui("message", c.room->self_id(), std::string_view(text), true);
    c.outgoing->async_send(std::move(text), [](boost::system::error_code ec) {
        if (ec) {
            ui("log", std::string_view("chat"), std::string_view("not delivered: " + ec.message()));
        }
    });
}

main keeps the chat, makes the page’s two calls, each a platform::page_call, which it hands to the page, and runs the io_context, under a work guard, for the page’s life. The page calls joinRoom and sendText from its own events, a form’s submission, and each call only posts its work to the io_context:

int main() {
    chat c;  // the page's one chat, which lives as long as the tab, in main's run
    // The page's two calls, functions of webcpp::asio's bridge that post their work to the
    // io_context: joinRoom with the form's app and room, sendText with the text its user wrote.
    const trystero::platform::page_call join(c.io.get_executor(),
                                             [&c](const val& form) { join_room(c, form); });
    const trystero::platform::page_call send(c.io.get_executor(),
                                             [&c](const val& text) { send_message(c, text); });
    val::global("chatUi").call<void>("ready", join.function(), send.function());
    // The page waits for its user with no work at all: the guard keeps the run going.
    const auto guard = webcpp::asio::make_work_guard(c.io);
    c.io.run();  // lint-run: the page's program, suspended into the browser's event loop
}

Any Trystero JS page, or any other page of the chat, that joins the same app and room is in the same chat (Running the examples).

The protocol

A room keeps Trystero 0.26.0’s wire byte for byte. The protocol’s pure functions are in <webcpp/trystero/protocol/>; their tests compare them, byte for byte, with values Trystero JS computed itself (Testing). What a Trystero JS peer or a page sees never changes: the topic prefixes Trystero@ and Trystero:, the handshake’s __trystero_pw, every constant and message layout, and the default relays in their order.

Discovery over Nostr

Part What it is

Root topic

Trystero’s sha1 of Trystero@<app>@<room>: each SHA-1 byte in base 36, unpadded, concatenated

Peer topic

the same of Trystero@<app>@<room>@<peer id>, where a peer receives its offers, answers and candidates

Event

kind 20000 plus the sum of the topic’s UTF-16 code units modulo 10000, ephemeral; the topic in an x tag; signed with BIP-340

Subscription

one per relay, to the root topic and the peer’s own topic

Announcement

{"peerId":...,"nonce":...} on the root topic: at once, then after 233, 533, 1333 and 5333 ms, then every 60 s

Relays

the configured ones, or 5 of Trystero’s 29 defaults, shuffled with sin(seed++) * 10000 seeded by the app id

A relay that answers rate-limited: is skipped for 60 s, doubling to 15 minutes while the replies persist; one that answers blocked:, restricted:, auth-required: or pow: is retired. A lost relay is reconnected after a random share of 3.3 s, doubling to 60 s, and the delay comes back to 3.3 s only once a connection stayed open for 60 s, so that a relay that closes the room at once after each open is tried less and less often.

A relay may repeat an event, and every relay of the room carries it, so a room acts on an event once: it remembers the ids of the newest 4096 events it received (detail::nostr_strategy::remembered_events) and drops one it remembers. An id is whatever a relay sends, so the room remembers one only once it has checked that it is the event’s own, the SHA-256 of the event’s NIP-01 serialization (protocol::nostr::has_own_id), and acts on an event whose id is not its own each time it comes, as Trystero acts on every event: a relay cannot have the room drop a genuine event by sending a forged one under its id first. The room indexes the ids with SipHash under a key it draws when it is made: no relay can choose ids that fall together, as it can in the standard library’s unseeded hash, where each lookup would walk all of them.

Signaling

Of two peers, the one with the lower id offers, on the relay that carried the other’s announcement. The higher one answers an announcement by announcing itself on the other’s peer topic, so the lower one offers: at most once a second per peer, and once in 5.3 s per relay for the whole room, Trystero’s announce interval, so that a flood of low ids does not have the relays rate-limit the room. Offers, answers and candidates are sealed with AES-GCM under the SHA-256 of <password>:<app>:<room>, using the immutable app_config::password, empty for a passwordless app, with a 16-byte IV, as the text <iv>$<ciphertext>: the IV’s bytes in decimal joined by commas, and the ciphertext with its tag in base64. Candidates follow their offer or answer, trickled. A negotiation ends when the data channel opens: the app adopts the connection, and signals from a bound peer are ignored. A live connection is reused for another room only after the peer advertised that room’s token itself on the connection.

JSON texts

Every JSON text a room reads or writes is webcpp::document’s. A text is read by webcpp::document::parse into a webcpp::document::pmr::document of the room’s resource, or of the app’s for a candidate, which holds its image and the parse’s working state, and read through its handles as views; a key written twice keeps its last value, as JSON.parse keeps it. Each caller bounds what it reads, as parse_options::max_bytes, and drops a longer text before reading it, as it drops a malformed one:

Text Bound Why

a relay’s text

68,608 bytes

an event that carries the longest signal, with 2 KiB for its other fields

a signal

66,560 bytes

a sealed offer or answer of 64 KiB with the longest ids, and 1 KiB to spare

a handshake message

1,024 bytes

ten times Trystero’s longest, 99 bytes

a remote candidate

16 KiB

the bound of a sealed candidate, which its opened JSON never passes

The image grows in place, twice as large each time, to at most twice the bound and 64 KiB (protocol::json::protocol_limits, as parse_options::max_document_bytes): a text Trystero writes holds a few dozen values, and a text of thousands of values, which would need a hundred times its length, is refused once its image has grown to that bound. A protocol text nests at most 16 deep (protocol::json::max_protocol_depth, as parse_options::max_depth), where Trystero’s nest 4 deep at most, so that a hostile relay’s text takes the parse’s recursion no deeper. A document keeps no hashed index, so no key read twice, or chosen to collide, makes a parse slower than the logarithm of its object’s size: no text costs a room more than a multiple of its bound to read.

A JSON payload, received as either document type, is read into an image of at most 96 times its length and 64 KiB (protocol::json::payload_limits): each value of a document is a node of 192 bytes, and one of a single character takes two bytes of text with its comma, so every valid payload fits. The room’s room_options::max_json_document_bytes, 64 MiB by default, bounds that image whatever the payload, so that a program bounds what a peer’s JSON may take of its room’s resource: some 350,000 values of one character pass the default (A JSON payload nested deeper than 256, holding a lone surrogate, or past the room’s bound). A payload’s other bounds are the room’s max_receive_bytes and document’s defaults, values nested at most 256 deep; and document refuses a lone surrogate, "\ud800", which JSON.parse takes. A payload past any of them is not delivered.

A parse recurses once a level of nesting. Under Asyncify, the build leaves Boost.JSON’s recursive descent, the parse_* functions of its basic_parser, out of Asyncify’s instrumentation (asyncify-remove.json, which /webcpp/trystero//trystero links), since none of them suspends: instrumented, a level took some 6.5 KB of the engine’s stack in a debug build before the engine optimized the code, so a peer’s first payload nested 256 deep overflowed node’s stack at about 150 levels; uninstrumented, it reaches 400, and in a release build more than 1,000. The room test sends such a payload first, in both suspension variants.

A text the protocol writes is a fixed shape of a few strings and numbers, appended field by field, its strings quoted by webcpp::document::quote, the bytes JSON.stringify writes. A string that is not UTF-8 cannot be quoted, and the writer returns that error: the only such string a program gives that is ever written, its self id, is set aside for a random one when the app is made, with a configuration report to app::on_error, and a local candidate whose text is not UTF-8, which no browser’s is, is not sent.

The data channel

Every message is a room frame: 1, the length of the room token (16 bits, big-endian), the token, the hexadecimal SHA-256 of Trystero:<app>:<room>, then an action frame. A presence frame, 2, present or not, the token’s length and the token, announces or withdraws the room.

Presence advertises every room of the app on each connection. It records which rooms the remote peer joined and binds matching local rooms; a withdrawal detaches only that room. The connection routes by token:

Frame What happens

An envelope that does not decode

The connection ends for every room.

presence(1, T), new token

Record it; a 65th distinct token ends the connection. Bind the matching local room when its binding conditions permit.

presence(1, T), known token

Bind the matching unbound local room when permitted.

presence(0, T)

Forget the token and its kept frames, and end its binding as a departure.

Room frame, token bound

Deliver it to that room’s action wire.

Room frame after the higher id’s own kick, before it sends presence

Drop it: it belongs to the ended binding.

Room frame for another room of the app, not bound to this connection

Keep it, at most 64 frames per connection, all expiring 10 s after the first, and record its token as the peer’s advertisement, below 64 tokens. Bind when no backoff runs.

Room frame for any other token

Drop it silently; keep the connection.

A room frame is the peer’s own advertisement of its room, as its presence is: only the peer writes to its connection. Trystero sends a room’s presence once per connection, from the open of the channel, and Chrome can drop what a page sends on an answering channel as it opens (its log says "Send failed INVALID_STATE"): a room waiting for that presence alone would never bind the peer, whose frames of the room keep coming.

On binding, kept frames arrive before later frames; a kept @_leave discards itself and everything kept before it for that token. There is no buffer for a bound room awaiting its handler: delivery is installed in the same call that makes its binding.

Waiting sends take turns by binding on each channel drain, preserving each binding’s waiter order and the 10 s stall bound. Chunked transfers send one chunk per drain, giving waiting sends from other rooms a turn. Inline sends at a buffered amount of at most 64 KiB go straight to the channel: they have no trystero rate bound, so a flood of pings can delay every room’s traffic to that peer, and that peer only.

Action frames are Trystero’s action wire, version 2: an inline frame carries the payload whole; a larger payload is an offer, accepted or refused by the receiver, then chunks of at most 16,370 bytes, in order. Integers and float64 values are big-endian, as JavaScript’s DataView writes them. An offer’s size is a float64 that must be a whole number from 1 to 253 - 1, JavaScript’s Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (protocol::max_offer_size), as Trystero checks it: any other makes the frame malformed, and the room kicks its sender, as Trystero does. The size is read in 64 bits on every target, so a 32-bit one too compares the whole size with max_receive_bytes, and refuses a transfer beyond it as Trystero does.

Frame Bytes

inline (kind 0)

2, the kind and the format shifted by four, the name (32 bytes, NUL padded), the metadata’s length (uint16), the metadata, the payload

offer (kind 1)

the inline header, the transfer’s id (uint32), the payload’s size (float64), the metadata

chunk (kind 2)

2, 2, the transfer’s id (uint32), the offset (float64), the bytes

accepted (kind 3)

2, 3, the transfer’s id (uint32)

rejected (kind 4)

2, 4, the transfer’s id (uint32), the reason (UTF-8, at most 200 bytes)

cancelled (kind 5)

2, 5, the transfer’s id (uint32)

The payload’s format is text (0), JSON (1) or binary (2). Internal actions run the room:

Action What it carries

@_hsdata

the password handshake: the lower id sends a challenge, and the other answers with the hexadecimal SHA-256 of <challenge>:<password>:<app>:<room>

@_hsready

the sender’s side of the handshake passed; a peer joins when both sides sent it

@_ping, @_pong

round trips

@_leave

the sender leaves the room

The media actions, @_stream, @_track and @_signal, are not ported (Differences from Trystero): a frame of one is ignored.

Bounded signaling

Announcements are not sealed, so anyone who knows the app and room ids can announce any number of peer ids, and anyone who reads the relays can send any signal in any peer’s name. Trystero JS bounds none of this; trystero bounds what each costs a room.

  • Nothing a peer sends changes a negotiation before it opens with the room key: an offer, an answer or a candidate that does not open is counted, reported once per negotiation, and changes nothing else. A flood of fresh ids makes each a negotiation, so the reports are paced: the first of a quiet 10 s goes to on_error at once, with its peer, and the others of those 10 s in one report, with no peer and their number.

  • A room holds at most detail::signaling::max_unconnected_peers (32) negotiations with peers it is not connected to. A negotiation whose offer and answer expire without a connection is dropped, an idle one gives its place to a new peer, and a new peer beyond the bound is refused and logged once. A negotiation is idle when it holds no connection and no offer of its peer is being opened: the one idle longest gives its place, and of those idle as long, as every negotiation is at one instant of a page’s coarse clock, the one the room took first. So an offer whose sealed text the backend is still opening (Web Crypto’s asynchronous step in a page) keeps its place however many new ids arrive meanwhile, and is acted on once it opens.

  • A negotiation opens one offer of its peer at a time, as Trystero answers one at a time: until it is opened, another offer in that name is ignored, and the same offer through another relay has the answer sent there too. So the room opens at most 32 offers at once, and offers sent in one name, however many, hold one open and one copy of an offer. As with Trystero, a forged offer opened first has the peer’s own, arriving meanwhile, wait until the peer sends it again, 2 s later.

  • A room makes at most max_connections_per_window (64) connections in any 57 s, however soon they end; the platform backend makes at most 256 a minute on both targets (Its configuration), and a page holds at most 256 (The runtime).

  • A signal’s fields are bounded in protocol/signal.hpp: the peer id (64 bytes; Trystero’s are 20), the offer id (64 bytes), a sealed offer or answer (64 KiB) and a sealed candidate (16 KiB, above the 8192 bytes of plaintext Trystero takes).

  • A relay is a third party too: its texts are bounded at 1 MiB, what the room holds unsent for it at 4 MiB, and, natively, its silence at 30 s (The relays).

Bound Scope Value and consequence

Joined rooms

App

64, counting farewells until withdrawal; join returns error::too_many_rooms beyond it.

Advertised room tokens

Connection

64 distinct tokens; a 65th ends the connection.

Kept frames for unbound local rooms

Connection

64, at most 64 x 16,515 bytes; expire together 10 s after the first. Other tokens retain nothing.

Room frame and token

Connection

16,515 bytes, token 1 to 128 bytes; an invalid envelope ends the connection.

No bindings

Connection

idle_timeout after a departure, 123,333 ms by default, 0 closes immediately; closed at once if its last binding was kicked.

Handshake

Room and peer

handshake_timeout, 10 s; failure kicks that binding only.

Earlier challenges

Room and peer

Last 8 since the last completed handshake; a correct answer to any passes.

Pending action frames

Room and peer

64 for 120 s; one incoming transfer per peer, max_receive_bytes across peers, and 1024 queued messages per action.

After a kick or the peer’s @_leave, a live connection is rebound one step after that binding ended. The initial step is the larger of handshake_timeout and 10 s, plus 1 s (11 s by default), doubling at each further end to 5 minutes. Only a completed handshake or the connection’s end resets it. After its own kicks the lower id refuses bindings until its backoff ends, ignores signals and keeps frames; the higher id drops frames until it next sends presence and accepts the lower id’s presence at once. The room sends presence again on reuse or scheduled rebinding, making the other side bind without a relay response. Announcements restart only when no live connection remains. A forged announcement never binds a peer that has not advertised that token itself.

A connection counts against its negotiating room’s 64-per-57-s window even after the app adopts it; presence and reuse make no connections. Fresh ids that connect and depart keep at most 64 x ceil(idle_timeout / 57 s) idle connections per room, 192 by default, within the backend’s own bound. Leaving a room with many peers retains no more connections than the app already held. Kept frames and tokens cost at most about 1 MiB and 8 KiB per connection; each of at most 64 bound rooms retains its own peer bounds. A flood spends its room’s queues, transfers and reservations; routing never holds one room’s frame for another room.

With the lower id an invalid room response proof causes at most six kicks and reports in the first ten minutes, then one per 5 minutes. The higher id can be rebound by a lower-id peer at that peer’s pace, but reports at most one handshake timeout per handshake_timeout, and does not verify a response proof. Malformed challenges are rejected by their receiver and can also report wrong_password; their report rate follows the malicious peer’s repeated bindings, rather than the timeout bound.

Replayed offers and answers

A sealed offer or answer holds neither its offer id nor a peer id (Trystero’s wire), so one recorded from the relays still opens when anyone resends it in its sender’s name, and so does the room’s own, sent back to it. A room remembers, by the SHA-256 of their opened text, the last 1024 offers and answers it made or acted on (detail::signaling::remembered_descriptions), and refuses one that comes to it as a peer’s: it changes nothing and is logged. It makes or acts on at most two per connection it makes, so each is remembered for at least an offer’s lifetime (57 s), and in a quiet room for its whole life. So a room refuses a sealed offer or answer it acted on, resent, and one it made itself, sent back as a peer’s offer or answer.

What remains

Sharing preserves Trystero JS 0.26.0’s wire. Each C++ app is one password domain: it copies one password at construction, and all its rooms use it. The initial sealed signaling authenticates that password before the data channel is adopted. Later room binding reuses this authenticated connection. There are no per-room overrides, and different passwords require separate apps with distinct self ids. This protects admission to the C++ app’s rooms without changing the room handshake on the wire.

A watcher not connected to the app, without the key, can keep two peers apart. A sealed offer or answer the room neither made nor acted on still opens and is acted on. Such texts are not scarce: every peer seals a fresh offer for any id announced above its own, and announcements need no key. So anyone who reads and publishes on the relays, without the key, can keep any two peers of a room apart from their first meeting for as long as it keeps at it, each attempt costing the other peer a connection of its window. A watcher not connected to the app cannot read or alter anything the peers exchange, join the room, or touch peers already joined; a joined peer that drops is a new peer again. The room refuses only what it made or already acted on. Only a wire that seals the offer id and both peer ids closes this, which Trystero would have to share (reported upstream).

A flooder can delay new peers. Joined peers, memory and connections stay safe under a flood, but a flooder who keeps sending new ids takes each place, or each connection of the window, as it frees, so new peers can be kept out for as long as the flood lasts, each place up to one offer’s lifetime (57 s) at a time. A joined peer whose connection drops comes back as a new peer, with the same id, and is kept out the same way: the room has no renegotiation that would keep its place. Closing it needs announcements that prove the room key, a wire change Trystero would have to share.

A passwordless app’s rooms are open to its connected peers. Presence gives a peer connected through any room the token of every room of that app. Relay events reveal their topics in the clear, and announcements reveal the app’s peer id. The token alone binds the existing connection, and the empty app password goes straight to @_hsready, so that peer can join another room without knowing its id. A watcher not connected to the app still needs the room id to derive its topics and signaling key. Protected rooms belong to another app with a password and a distinct self id. Its presence, tokens and connections never reach the passwordless app.

The upstream one-way handshake remains. The responder to a room challenge answers and passes its side; only the lower id verifies the password proof. A Trystero JS page that itself mixes different passwords on one app’s shared connection can therefore admit a peer to its own higher-id room without that room’s password, and can expose a challenge response for offline guessing. The C++ app-domain boundary does not repair such a JS page. Configure all rooms of one JS app with one password, and use separate page contexts for different password domains. The wire has not gained bilateral room proofs.

A domain member can send an invalid room proof. A peer already connected to a protected C++ app knows its domain password from the initial sealed negotiation. It can nevertheless answer a later room’s challenge incorrectly or send malformed handshake data. The room kicks that binding and applies the documented backoff; only the lower id checks and reports a wrong response. These checks isolate faulty peers within an authenticated domain, rather than admitting another password domain.

One identity links the app’s rooms. Each room announces the same peerId in clear, and connected peers see it across shared rooms. Relay observers and peers can link those rooms to one program. Separate apps provide separate identities and connections for rooms that must remain unlinked. A forged announcement in a connected peer’s name binds nothing: only the peer itself, on its encrypted connection, can advertise the token. It causes no report or rebinding count against that innocent peer.

Two transient cases remain with a Trystero JS lower id. If it binds by reuse during the higher C++ id’s dropping window, its challenge is dropped and its handshake can time out once. With the default 10 s timeout the next rebinding joins by at most 43 s after the first kick plus one-way delay, with no false password error on either side. If a JS page’s timer that expires a stale answer runs later than the 1 s margin before presence arrives, JS can flush the old answer into a new handshake and report a false password error. One-minute timer lag can repeat this at the 11, 22 and 44 s steps, at most three times, before the 88 s step exceeds that lag. The C++ side reports nothing false in either case.

Design

Layers

Layer Headers Knows

Protocol

protocol/*.hpp

pure functions over bytes and text: no I/O, no platform

Backend interface

backend.hpp

the WebSocket, peer connection, data channel, timer and AES-GCM sealer a platform provides

App

app.hpp, detail/app_impl.hpp, detail/connection.hpp

one identity, the room registry, shared connections and their routing

Room

room.hpp, detail/*.hpp

the Nostr strategy, signaling, bindings, action wire and room API

Backend’s WebRTC

webrtc/*.hpp

webcpp::webrtc’s peer connections and data channels, and trystero’s policies over them, on both targets

Platform backend

platform/*.hpp

webcpp::webrtc, webcpp::beast (natively Boost.Beast, in a page its WebSocket), Boost.URL, webcpp::asio’s timers, and per target the sealer and the randomness: OpenSSL natively, Web Crypto and crypto.getRandomValues in a page; and, in a page, page_call and js_string

Everything above the backend interface is the core, which builds on both targets: the same room runs over the browser’s WebRTC and libdatachannel’s, both through webcpp::webrtc, and over the memory relays of the tests (Testing). The core never includes the platform backend, the backend’s WebRTC, webcpp::webrtc, libdatachannel, OpenSSL or Emscripten: a boundary of the library’s own, which webcpp’s lint checks, keeps it so. Its Asio is webcpp::asio: natively Boost.Asio itself, on emscripten the backend webcpp::asio ships, whose io_context webcpp::webrtc’s browser objects deliver their events to.

Connections shared by the rooms of an app

Object Owns Lives Resource

app

A reference to detail::app_impl, counted as one user

While the user keeps its handle

None

Room’s, the app’s by default

  • A room holds the app strongly; the app reaches rooms weakly. A binding holds its connection weakly, and the connection holds plain pointers to bindings. Detachment removes those pointers and every drain registration before returning. Ending a room removes its registry entry, so the app keeps no allocation of that room’s resource after it ends, and no cycle keeps the objects alive.

  • Sharing is scoped by the app the user constructs, with no registry outside it and no static state keyed by the backend. Two apps with the same application id in one process are two peers. Each app has one immutable password. Different passwords use separate apps with distinct self ids, so their connections, tokens and presence are never reused.

  • The action wire continues to write its room token and send through a channel_link. The binding implements that link: each room keeps its own actions, transfers, queues and bounds.

Why abstract classes for the backend

The backend is a handful of abstract classes rather than template parameters. Each of its operations is a call into JavaScript or into a network stack, so a virtual call costs nothing measurable, while the room’s code stays free of templates over the platform and of #ifdef, and the tests’ memory relays and the platform backend are interchangeable at run time. Every handler a backend invokes runs on the room’s executor, after the call that caused it has returned, never inside it: the room calls these operations from inside handlers whose state a completion run there would change under them.

One class, platform::backend, implements the interface on both targets, in place of a backend of each: the owner’s decision 3 of trystero’s refactor (2026-11-14), since webcpp::asio, webcpp::beast and webcpp::webrtc give both targets one interface, where everything but WebRTC was written twice. The abstract classes stay, for the memory relays, which run whole rooms on both targets where node has no WebRTC, and for the interop’s native peer, which wraps the platform backend. Only the sealer and the source of randomness are chosen per target, by WEBCPP_TARGET_EMSCRIPTEN, until webcpp::crypto exists (The platform backend).

Why webcpp::webrtc

The platform backend’s WebRTC is webcpp::webrtc’s: the W3C’s API in Asio’s model, one interface natively, over libdatachannel’s C API, and in the browser, over the page’s own RTCPeerConnection. It replaces the backend’s own wrappers of each, so that trystero keeps only its policies over WebRTC, the same on both targets. In the browser it binds the page’s objects, not libdatachannel’s WebAssembly port, datachannel-wasm, which has no media and hides the RTCPeerConnection it wraps; natively its C API lets the backend work without exceptions. The backend interface stays a handful of abstract classes (Why abstract classes for the backend): the rooms of the tests run over the memory relays, on both targets, where node has no WebRTC, and the interop’s native peer wraps the platform backend’s connections.

The backend’s WebRTC

The platform backend makes its peer connections and data channels the same way on both targets, in <webcpp/trystero/webrtc/peer_connection.hpp> and data_channel.hpp: webrtc::peer_connection and webrtc::data_channel hold webcpp::webrtc’s basic_peer_connection and basic_data_channel over a std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator on the app’s resource, keep a wait of each kind pending on them, re-armed on the executor, and report what each completes with through the backend interface. What is trystero’s, and stays in them, over webcpp::webrtc:

  • The states. A connection reports one state, which merges its connection state and its ICE state as a page sees both: failed when either failed, then closed, disconnected, connected (or ICE completed), connecting (or ICE checking), and new.

  • The candidates. A local candidate leaves as the JSON of an RTCIceCandidateInit, the form Trystero JS adds with addIceCandidate; a remote one is read from that JSON, at most 16 KiB of it. Natively it carries sdpMid and an sdpMLineIndex of 0, and no user name fragment, as libdatachannel gives none; a candidate whose text is not UTF-8, which JSON cannot carry, is not reported.

  • The frames. A channel reads every message as it comes, with async_receive, into a vector of the app’s resource, which the message handler then owns. A text message, as a peer can send, or a binary one larger than any room frame, is dropped there, on the executor: neither can be a frame. What reaches the executor is bounded by webcpp::webrtc: a message is at most max_message_size, 256 KiB, which natively libdatachannel cuts a longer one to, and past which in the browser, or past 16 MiB of unread messages, the channel closes. A binary payload moves when its message buffer and the room use the same resource, and is copied once otherwise; chunked transfers assemble their buffer in the room’s resource.

  • The frames no room has read. Valid binary frames that arrive before the message handler is installed wait in a FIFO in the app’s resource. The queue holds at most 64 frames for at most 10 seconds from its first frame, Trystero’s pending-data bounds. Overflow or expiry closes the channel; closing or destroying it discards the pending frames. The backend’s timer invalidates an expiry already queued when the queue drains or closes. Installing a receiver posts delivery on the executor with the app’s allocator. It never calls the receiver inline, and delivery checks the current handler and channel before each frame, so a handler may replace itself or close the channel. A message already read ahead of that delivery drains older frames first when a receiver is available.

  • The pace. The channel reports the buffered amount falling to 64 KiB, after a send left it above, as onbufferedamountlow does.

  • The caps. The backend makes at most backend_config::max_peer_connections_per_minute connections in any minute, on both targets, its own policy against floods (Its configuration): in a page a collection frees closed connections from the census, after which only this window bounds how fast a flood makes new ones. The runtime of webcpp::webrtc caps the connections alive at once, the backend’s own or the program’s (The runtime), in a page over the page’s census (What a page bounds).

Text is a view, a copy is a decision

A parameter that only reads text is a std::string_view, bytes are a std::span, and a string is used where something must own the text: a map key, a member, a capture of a handler that runs later.

  • The digests the protocol takes are fed the parts of their input: nothing is concatenated to hash it.

  • Every JSON text is webcpp::document’s. Signals, relay messages, handshake messages and candidates are parsed by webcpp::document::parse into a webcpp::document::pmr::document of the room’s or the app’s resource, which holds its image and the parse’s working state, and read as views into it; each caller bounds its text, and the image grows to at most twice that bound and 64 KiB (JSON texts). The JSON the room writes goes field by field into one reserved buffer, its strings quoted by webcpp::document::quote, the quoting of JSON.stringify itself, and a Nostr event’s id is hashed over those same bytes. Building each text as a document and writing it again was set aside: it would copy every string into a node of some 200 bytes, then write it once more. trystero keeps no owner of its own around a document: an earlier one, a buffer of the room’s resource under an external document, retried twice as large when a parse filled it, gave way to document’s own allocator, whose image grows in place.

  • A JSON payload is a document of document’s own types, webcpp::document::document in the standard allocator, the user’s choice, and webcpp::document::pmr::document, received in the room’s resource, as a text is a std::string or a std::pmr::string. A handle keeps document’s rule: it refers to its document object, and moving the document invalidates it.

  • A frame is written once, inside its room envelope, and shared by every target; a received frame becomes the buffer of the message delivered from it, and a view handler reads it in place.

  • A sentence of the log is composed only when there is a sink.

The asynchronous operations are the exception, for the reason Completion tokens and ownership gives.

Dependencies

trystero builds on webcpp::asio, and its platform backend on webcpp::webrtc and webcpp::beast. /webcpp/trystero//trystero is the rooms alone: it brings /webcpp/asio//asio, which links embind on emscripten, and on no target webcpp::webrtc. A program names /webcpp/trystero//platform on both targets, which adds the backend to the rooms: /webcpp/webrtc//webrtc and /webcpp//boost_url on both; natively webcpp::webrtc’s libdatachannel, under the MPL 2.0, and OpenSSL, under the Apache License 2.0, and for the relays /webcpp/beast//tls and /webcpp/asio//tls, whose embedded authorities a program may trust in place of the system’s; in a page /webcpp/beast//browser, over the page’s WebSocket. Neither libdatachannel nor OpenSSL is in a page’s program, as OpenSSL is optional for Asio.

Licensing

The library is distributed under the Boost Software License. It ports Trystero’s protocol and was written with Trystero’s source open, so Trystero’s MIT notice comes with it (Acknowledgements).

Guarantees

What trystero promises, and the test that holds each promise, which fails when the promise breaks. A guarantee keeps its number, and the anchor named after it, so a comment of the code or of a test cites it by that anchor: (doc: #trystero-invariant-3) sends its reader to the third. b2 libs/trystero/doc, which builds this page, fails on a citation that names no anchor of it. The tests are those of Testing.

  1. The wire is Trystero 0.26.0’s. A C++ peer, in the browser or native, and Trystero JS peers in one room join, exchange text, JSON and binary messages, files both ways with metadata, and pings, leave, and form a mesh, with either side offering. Held by the interop lane, interop_browser on emscripten and interop_native natively, against Trystero 0.26.0 itself in headless Chrome.

  2. Every protocol value equals Trystero JS’s. Topics, room tokens, the relay shuffle, sealed text, Nostr event ids, inline and chunked action frames, control frames, envelopes and presence are what Trystero’s own functions compute from the same inputs, byte for byte. Held by protocol, against the values the oracle lane has Trystero 0.26.0 write, and by the oracle lane, which fails when Trystero would write other values than those committed; and by platform_sealer, natively and on emscripten, which opens what Trystero JS sealed with Web Crypto.

  3. A peer with another password never joins a protected C++ app’s rooms. Its initial signals do not open under the app’s password, so it obtains no shared connection into that domain. Every room of that app uses the same immutable password. This promise concerns the C++ app’s admission; an upstream JS page that mixes passwords retains its one-way handshake exposure (What remains). Held by room (the_same_password_joins_and_another_does_not), platform_room (another_password_never_joins), and password-domain tests of shared and interop.

  4. A payload larger than a frame travels in chunks, both ways. It is offered, accepted and sent in chunks of at most 16,370 bytes, and arrives whole, from either peer. Held by room (large_payloads_travel_in_chunks_both_ways, 100 KB each way), and the file transfers of the interop lane.

  5. Every allocation of an app and its rooms goes through their resources, but what What stays outside the resource lists: from its construction until its io_context has drained, neither the global operator new nor the C library sees an allocation, while its rooms read and write their JSON texts and exchange text, binary and JSON payloads of the std::pmr types and webcpp::document::pmr::document; over the platform backend’s relays, natively a message adds nothing, and in a page each event of a relay’s WebSocket adds embind’s string of the event’s type, two for a message. Held by allocation, natively and on emscripten; for a page’s sealer, platform_page_sealer_allocation; and for the relays, platform_websocket_allocation natively and platform_page_relay_allocation in a page, which counts exactly what is listed.

  6. No unit test reaches beyond the loopback. The rooms of the unit tests meet over the memory relays, the native tests’ peer connections bind to 127.0.0.1 and gather their candidates there alone, and the WebSocket test talks to a server of its own on 127.0.0.1. Held by the container lanes, gcc-14 and clang-linux-18: every unit test, built with GCC 14 and with clang 18 against libstdc++, passes in a Linux container that has no network but the loopback (docker run with the network none).

  7. A room refuses a replayed or reflected offer or answer. A sealed offer or answer it made, or acted on, that comes back to it as a peer’s changes nothing (Replayed offers and answers). Held by room (a_replayed_answer_is_refused, a_replayed_offer_is_refused, a_reflected_offer_is_refused_as_an_answer, a_reflected_offer_is_refused_as_an_offer and a_reflected_answer_is_refused_as_an_answer), and the replay and reflection scenarios of the interop lane.

  8. A relay that stops reading is dropped. Once the text held unsent for it would pass 4 MiB, the connection is dropped, and reports one close, after which the room reconnects with its backoff, as it does to any relay that closes. Held by platform_websocket (a_relay_that_stops_reading_is_dropped_at_the_queue_bound, a close before 2000 texts of 64 KiB, and one only) natively, and on emscripten, with exceptions and without them, by platform_page_websocket_bound, where the page’s WebSocket holds what is unsent, which also checks that it never holds more than 4 MiB, and platform_page_websocket_late_events, where the session’s queue does, which checks one close and no message after it; the reconnection by room (a_relay_that_closes_at_once_is_tried_less_and_less_often).

  9. One connection per remote peer per app is shared by its rooms. Each room keeps its own membership and actions on that connection. Held by shared, cases 1 to 3, and the interop’s first shared scenario.

  10. A room’s departure leaves the app’s other rooms joined. They continue sending over the same connection. Held by shared, case 8, and shared interop scenario 5, with either side leaving.

  11. Different passwords share no C++ app connection or presence. Protected rooms use a separate app with a distinct self id; a peer of a passwordless app gains no binding to that protected app by echoing tokens. Held by the password-domain cases of shared and shared interop scenario 4.

Testing

Testing a program that uses trystero

A room needs relays and peers, and a test needs neither the network nor another machine. The backend interface is the seam: a program’s tests run its rooms over a backend of their own, in memory, as trystero’s own tests run whole rooms over test/support/memory_backend.hpp, a backend whose Nostr relays forward ephemeral events to matching subscriptions, whose peer connections pair through their descriptions, whose data channels deliver in order, and whose sealer opens only what was sealed under the same key, each event posted to the io_context. It is in the namespace webcpp::trystero::test, outside the library’s public headers, and a program may copy it.

The memory network identifies connection ends with std::size_t ids. on_made records construction and ICE servers, and peer_of identifies the paired end. A filter delivers, drops or holds frames; a held frame holds all later frames from its sending end behind it, preserving channel order until release. Deferred open calls open each end separately; inject and fail supply malformed frames and transport failure. With hold_sealer_opens, every sealer’s opens wait, as Web Crypto’s take their time in a page, until release_sealer_opens completes them in order; held_sealer_opens counts them.

With channel_capacity enabled, the channel queues bytes and drains up to drain_per_post per post. It delivers a frame only after its last byte drains, and buffered reports the exact unsent amount. Set virtual_clock before making timers: advance fires due timers in order and runs ready work between them; step and poll_ready give tests finer control. Timeouts, backoffs and late frames are tested without wall-clock sleeps. Optional fault hooks allocate outside the measured resources only when enabled; the allocation test leaves them disabled.

A native test of the platform backend’s own WebRTC binds its connections to the loopback, platform::backend_config::bind_address set to "127.0.0.1", and names a STUN server where nothing answers, stun:127.0.0.1:9, in place of Trystero’s public ones: the loopback’s host candidate is then the only one, and it is enough. A page cannot bind, and leaves bind_address empty (Its configuration).

How trystero is tested

trystero’s tests are under test/, each declared in test/Jamfile, and each guarantee of Guarantees names the tests that hold it. They run on two targets: 109 tests in all, 79 natively and 87 on emscripten, under node, each in both of webcpp::asio’s suspension variants, JSPI and Asyncify. The protocol, the rooms, the timer and the allocation test run on both:

webcpp.run protocol : protocol_test.cpp : <testing.input-file>fixtures/expected/expected.json ;
# The signaling and the Nostr strategy alone: an answerer's signals against
# Trystero's, and the bounds of the texts they read.
webcpp.run signaling : signaling_test.cpp
  : <testing.input-file>fixtures/expected/expected.json ;
webcpp.run room : room_test.cpp ;
# Rooms of one app that share one connection per remote peer; once as the
# build asks, once without exceptions, on both targets; and, natively, once
# with the standard libraries' checks, so that a kept frame that kicks during
# a binding, or a waiter failed during a connection's end, fails at once when
# it touches what it removed.
webcpp.run shared : shared_test.cpp ;
webcpp.run shared_no_exceptions : shared_test.cpp : <exception-handling>off ;
webcpp.run shared_hardened : shared_test.cpp
  : <define>_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_EXTENSIVE <define>_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS
  : native ;
# The memory backend's hooks, which the tests of shared connections drive.
webcpp.run memory_backend : memory_backend_test.cpp ;
# The shared connection alone, over a memory pair.
webcpp.run connection : connection_test.cpp ;
# The state an app and its rooms share, alone, over the memory backend.
webcpp.run app_impl : app_impl_test.cpp ;
# The timer over webcpp::asio's steady_timer, which the platform backend
# makes: a wait cancelled, restarted or destroyed never fires.
webcpp.run timer : timer_test.cpp : $(part) ;
webcpp.run allocation : allocation_test.cpp : <toolset>emscripten:<linkflags>-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH ;

The timer’s test, of a part that parses no JSON, links parts ($(part)) in place of the rooms, the Jamfile’s own requirement, without their Asyncify list (In a b2 project).

Test What it checks

the public headers

Each compiled alone, on each target that builds it: the core, and the platform backend’s backend.hpp, entropy.hpp, sealer.hpp and websocket.hpp with the backend’s WebRTC, on both, natively against webcpp::webrtc’s libdatachannel and OpenSSL and in a page over its own objects; and platform/page.hpp, on emscripten alone.

config, config_developer_defined, config_all_off

<webcpp/trystero/config.hpp> defines WEBCPP_TRYSTERO_NO_EXCEPTIONS exactly when webcpp has no exceptions (WEBCPP_HAS_EXCEPTIONS is not defined: the compiler has none, or the program defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS), and keeps it when a developer defines it for trystero alone in a build that has them.

protocol

The protocol against values Trystero JS 0.26.0 computed itself: topics, room tokens, the relay shuffle, sealed text, Nostr event ids, inline and chunked action frames, control frames, envelopes and presence, a JSON payload’s numbers and key order, and the bounds of a signal’s fields.

signaling

The signaling and the Nostr strategy alone: as an answerer, the signals Trystero JS 0.26.0’s own signal handler published for the same offers, byte for byte, a signal or a relay’s text read at its bound and dropped one byte past it, and a relay’s text read 16 deep and dropped one level deeper.

room, room_asyncify_release

Whole rooms in one process, over the memory relays: every payload format, 100 KB transfers both ways, ping, passwords right and wrong, leaving and returning, a room moved over a joined one, ICE servers checked as WebRTC checks them, floods of announcements and of forged, replayed and reflected signals, offers being opened that keep their places when new ids arrive at the same instant, one offer of a peer opened at a time, a relay that closes at once or rate-limits, a three-peer mesh, coroutines and view handlers, JSON payloads read in the room’s resource up to its bound, and a rejected document receive.

app_impl, app_impl_asyncify_release

Configuration copying and validation, a self id that is not UTF-8 set aside, resource ownership, weak room registration, shared adoption, stale replacement, reentrant adoption, last-user closure and quiet destruction with pending work.

connection

Shared transport routing, advertised token and kept-frame limits, binding detachment, departures and kicks, idle expiry and drain ordering.

memory_backend

Virtual timer ordering, cancellation, held-frame order, deferred opens, injection and failures, and byte-accurate buffering and drain.

shared, shared_no_exceptions, shared_hardened

Multiple apps and rooms with one connection per remote peer, adoption races, presence and reuse, room isolation, departures, idle connections, password-domain isolation, invalid room proofs, transient handshake recovery, fairness, bounds, a handshake message read at its bound and failing one byte past it, and resource ownership. The suite also runs without exceptions and with standard-library hardening; sanitizers check lifetimes and detachment.

allocation, allocation_asyncify_release

Every allocation of two apps and their rooms goes through their resources (The proof).

timer

The timer over webcpp::asio’s steady_timer, which the platform backend makes on both targets: a wait fires once, in the timer’s resource, and one cancelled, restarted or destroyed never fires, even when its expiry was already queued.

platform_backend, platform_sealer, platform_websocket_unreachable, platform_websocket_url, and each _no_exceptions

The platform backend on both targets, natively and on emscripten under node, which has the page’s WebSocket and Web Crypto but no WebRTC. The backend itself keeps its own state, its copy of bind_address, its window of constructions and its own runtime, in backend_config::memory, none of it in the default resource, and gives it all back when it is destroyed (The app’s resource, the room’s and the backend’s); its clocks are the standard library’s, its randomness fills what it is given, differently each time, beyond a piece of its source too (65536 bytes in a page), its executor is the one it was given and its TLS context is made. The sealer opens what Trystero JS sealed with Web Crypto, seals a text that opens again in Trystero’s form, takes a text sealed under another key, or no sealed text, for a wrong password, completes after the call that started it, never inside it, and completes each of two seals and two opens given in one call, which in a page wait while it imports its key; in a page without crypto.subtle it fails with error::backend_failure. A relay it cannot reach, of a URL the session refuses, http:// and https:// among them, reports exactly one close, after the call that made it, and so does one of a port on 127.0.0.1 or ::1 where nothing listens, which is attempted: natively its TCP connection fails, and in a page node’s WebSocket is made and closes before it opens. A relay’s URL is read as a page reads it, and what a page’s URL parser reads otherwise is refused, by the same rules on both targets.

platform_websocket

The relays’ WebSocket natively, built with the standard libraries’ checks, against Beast servers in the same process: it opens, sends in order, closes once, reaches a relay at an IPv6 address (where the kernel opens a socket of IPv6’s family; elsewhere the case prints that it does not apply and checks nothing), opens over TLS with the relay’s name sent (SNI) against a test authority, refuses a certificate for another name or of an authority not trusted, also with a program’s context whose verify mode is verify_none, keeps a TLS context’s error in the backend, drops a binary message, closes once when the connection ends during a write, and drops a relay that sends too much, stops reading or stops answering, while one that answers its pings stays.

platform_websocket_allocation, platform_websocket_allocation_no_exceptions

Natively, a relay’s message allocates nothing outside the room’s resource: from the send of a text to the receipt of its echo, ten times, the global operator new counts none on the room’s thread (What stays outside the resource); and a relay that refuses the upgrade with a body of 4 MiB has its response’s header read alone, the room’s thread allocating less than 64 KiB until the close.

platform_peer_connection, platform_room, and each _no_exceptions

Natively, two connections of the backend’s WebRTC, over webcpp::webrtc’s libdatachannel, wired to each other, each handler on the executor, and whole rooms over the platform backend and real connections, bound to 127.0.0.1. A controlled executor holds the offerer’s events to prove pre-handler FIFO delivery, a 65th message read ahead of the posted flush, handler replacement and destruction, the 64-frame and 10-second bounds, and allocation and release through the connection’s resource; a peer of webcpp::webrtc’s own sends a text, which is dropped between two frames; malformed candidates and descriptions fail without throwing, and so does a candidate one byte past its bound, which at the bound is added; a local candidate that is not UTF-8 is not written; the backend makes at most its budget in a minute, holds at most its runtime’s cap at once, and leaves out a URL libdatachannel cannot parse. Both run once more without exceptions.

platform_page_websocket_bound, platform_page_websocket_late_events, platform_page_websocket_ingress, platform_page_websocket_tls, platform_page_data_channel, platform_page_peer_connection, platform_page, platform_page_call, platform_page_handlers, platform_page_sealer, platform_page_sealer_allocation, platform_page_relay_allocation, and each _no_exceptions

The platform backend in a page, on emscripten under node, each test’s main running its io_context as a page’s program does: the relays’ WebSocket, its bound on what a relay holds unsent, both the session’s own queue and the page’s bufferedAmount, which webcpp::beast’s send limit bounds, and its silence once dropped; its refusal of a text past 1 MiB that a relay sends in the same task as its open, and of a binary message; a program’s context of tls_client, whose verify mode is verify_none, reaching a wss:// relay, and the contexts a page cannot honour refused; what a relay’s connection and each of its messages allocate outside the room’s resource, exactly; over webcpp::webrtc’s browser objects and a page’s RTCPeerConnection of the test’s, a data channel’s refusal of what is no frame, and the page’s peer connections, made or refused, webcpp::webrtc’s census of them and the backend’s window of constructions, which holds in a page as natively; and the shape of a page’s program, whose work guard keeps a page with no room yet running, and whose platform::page_call functions, called from JavaScript while run is suspended, return at once, only post, and reach the room, twice in a row under Asyncify too, while a value of the wrong type is ignored and breaks nothing; a call through a function the page kept after its page_call, or its io_context, was destroyed reaches nothing, and the handler reads the page’s value as it is when it runs, and a number within its range; the relay socket’s and the sealer’s handlers run outside the page’s events; a page whose crypto.getRandomValues throws or is missing has no randomness and fails a seal, and one whose crypto.subtle settles with something other than an ArrayBuffer fails a seal and an open, with error::backend_failure, no JavaScript exception entering WebAssembly; and a seal and an open allocate nothing outside the room’s resource, neither with operator new nor with the C library’s functions.

The platform backend’s tests run on each target that builds them, and once more without exceptions (Exceptions), as a program that uses the backend may be built, but for platform_websocket, which runs once, with the standard libraries’ checks. The tests of a relay’s URL, a page’s calls and the sealer in a page, parts that parse no JSON, link platform-parts ($(platform-part)) in place of the backend and the rooms:

webcpp.run platform_backend : platform_backend_test.cpp : $(platform) ;
webcpp.run platform_sealer : platform_sealer_test.cpp

webcpp.run platform_websocket_unreachable : platform_websocket_unreachable_test.cpp
  : $(platform) ;

webcpp.run platform_websocket : platform_websocket_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <define>_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_EXTENSIVE
    <define>_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS
  : native ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket_allocation : platform_websocket_allocation_test.cpp
  : $(platform) : native ;
webcpp.run platform_peer_connection : platform_peer_connection_test.cpp
  : $(platform) : native ;
webcpp.run platform_room : platform_room_test.cpp : $(platform) : native ;
webcpp.run platform_backend_no_exceptions : platform_backend_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <exception-handling>off ;
webcpp.run platform_sealer_no_exceptions : platform_sealer_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <testing.input-file>fixtures/expected/expected.json <exception-handling>off ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket_unreachable_no_exceptions : platform_websocket_unreachable_test.cpp
  : $(platform) <exception-handling>off ;
webcpp.run platform_websocket_url_no_exceptions : platform_websocket_url_test.cpp
