Under Asyncify each suspension saves the frames from main down to the call that suspends, in webcpp::asio’s 8,192 bytes (webcpp::asio’s guide, "Asyncify’s stack"). A room’s own work is never among those frames (What a page needs), but a test’s cases are: each case calls the run family itself. So a test whose cases suspend runs each through webcpp::test::run_case (test/cases.hpp), in a frame of its own, which the frame of main never holds, whatever the link. At -O3 a case that main alone calls is inlined into it, and a program linked without optimization, as b2 linked a release build until 2026-11-15 and as <linkflags>-O0 still links one, then saves every case’s locals in the frame of main at each suspension: the room test’s main saved 29,776 bytes so, and the test stopped at its first suspension. b2 links a release build at -O3 now, where even a main with every case inlined fits, and the deepest build is debug. The room, app_impl and allocation tests, whose cases hold whole apps, run once more under Asyncify in a release build, as a page ships them, in the own lane asyncify on emscripten, which the CI’s emscripten lane, building JSPI, runs no other way (a target that names <webcpp-suspend>asyncify belongs in a lane of emscripten’s, since a build with no emscripten configured cannot expand that feature); their deepest suspensions wrote 564, 440 and 408 bytes there, and 2,344, 2,068 and 2,020 in debug (measured on 2026-11-15 with Emscripten 6.0.11):

webcpp.run room_asyncify_release : room_test.cpp
  : <webcpp-suspend>asyncify <variant>release : emscripten ;
webcpp.run app_impl_asyncify_release : app_impl_test.cpp
  : <webcpp-suspend>asyncify <variant>release : emscripten ;
webcpp.run allocation_asyncify_release : allocation_test.cpp
  : <webcpp-suspend>asyncify <variant>release <linkflags>-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH
  : emscripten ;
webcpp.lane asyncify : room_asyncify_release app_impl_asyncify_release
  allocation_asyncify_release : emscripten ;

From the root of a webcpp checkout, with libsecp256k1 found (Building), each of these builds and runs the tests, natively, under AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and on emscripten:

b2 libs/trystero/test
b2 libs/trystero/test address-sanitizer=norecover undefined-sanitizer=norecover
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/trystero/test

The chat page’s program is linked and never run, since it is a page; the quick start and the programs of the appendix "Differences" run over a relay of their own in the lane relayed (The examples over a relay, and their twins), and the one of them that needs no relay with the ordinary examples, b2 libs/trystero/example. b2 compares timestamps, so a result that counts is built from scratch, with b2 -a.

The oracle and the interop lanes

Two lanes of trystero’s own, declared in test/oracle/Jamfile, check it against Trystero itself, pinned at 0.26.0 by test/oracle/package.json and package-lock.json, with Node, run as node --conditions=development:

webcpp.original node --conditions=development ;
webcpp.twins ../../example : twins : .mjs : $(ORACLE)/run_twin.mjs ;
webcpp.cases protocol : oracle.mjs : ../fixtures/cases : ../fixtures/expected ;
webcpp.lane oracle : twins cases-protocol ;

oracle, which names no target, runs Trystero’s own functions over the inputs of test/fixtures/cases/protocol.json and checks that they still write test/fixtures/expected/expected.json byte for byte, the values the protocol and platform_sealer tests reproduce, and runs the twins of the examples (The examples over a relay, and their twins); update-expected is the only writer of the expected values and of each divergent twin’s output.

webcpp.drive interop_browser : interop/peer.cpp
  : <library>/webcpp/trystero//platform <linkflags>-sENVIRONMENT=web
    <linkflags>-sALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH <webcpp-drive-timeout>2400
  : interop/run.mjs : --browser : emscripten ;
webcpp.drive interop_native : interop/native_peer.cpp
  : <library>/webcpp/trystero//platform <threading>multi <webcpp-drive-timeout>2400
    <define>_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE=_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE_EXTENSIVE
    <define>_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS
  : interop/run.mjs : --native : native ;
webcpp.lane interop : interop_browser interop_native : native emscripten ;

interop, natively and on emscripten, meets each C++ peer, the native one as a process and the browser’s in headless Chrome, with Trystero JS peers in Chrome, over an in-memory Nostr relay on 127.0.0.1 that verifies every event’s id and signature as a public relay does. Its scenarios: the C++ peer offering; Trystero JS offering, with a password; a Trystero JS peer that also sends malformed candidates, or text messages on its data channel; a first relay to which no WebSocket can be made; a C++ peer given a TURN server without credentials; a watcher without the key that answers every offer with garbage in the other peer’s name, that resends a sealed answer and offer it recorded, and that sends the C++ peer its own sealed offer back, which the C++ peer must refuse; a flood of announcements and of unsealed offers from fresh peer ids; a relay text longer than 1 MiB; a C++ peer and a Trystero JS page each in two rooms of one app, sharing one connection and one peer id per app; a wrong password; and a mesh of three. The native peer meets three more: a room moved over the joined one, which must leave it as destroying it does; a relay that ends the connection just as the peer writes, which twelve peers in turn must survive; and the driver’s own check that a peer killed by a signal is named at once.

The shared-connection scenarios run in both lanes:

  1. Two rooms exchange chat and 100 KB files both ways on one adopted, connected transport.

  2. A third room joins later through presence on that transport.

  3. Rooms the JS page joined first bind when the C++ app joins them later.

  4. A peer can enter another room of a passwordless app by token, while a protected app with another password and self id shares no connection or presence with it, in either id order.

  5. Either side leaves one room while the other keeps exchanging, making no connection.

  6. Leaving every room closes the transport after the configured idle time.

  7. An authenticated peer sending wrong room proofs in both id orders gives paced lower-id reports while the other room keeps exchanging over the same connection.

  8. A 5,000-message flood in one room leaves pings in another completing within 2 s.

  9. A held handshake frame recovers in both id orders after one timeout, without a false password report; the other room keeps exchanging.

The C++ peers accept room2Delay and room3Delay in milliseconds; the JS page also accepts room2Delay. These delayed joins establish the first room before a shared-binding scenario begins; the proof-pacing scenario first authenticates the shared password domain, then corrupts room proofs after the initial announcement burst.

The adoption scenarios allow a crossed pair of connections to resolve, but fail with connection counts if either side constructs more than four. Transient recovery accounts for JS reuse during the higher id’s dropping window (What remains).

Every peer gathers its ICE candidates on the machine alone: the C++ peers get stun:127.0.0.1:9 in place of Trystero’s public STUN servers, the native peer binds its connections to 127.0.0.1, and the Trystero JS peers have no ICE server. Chrome is the one CHROME names, else on macOS Playwright’s chrome-headless-shell; the continuous integration names Chrome for Testing’s chrome-headless-shell, at the version webcpp pins. Each driver is bounded by 2,400 s, beyond its scenarios’ own limits, so that a scenario that does not complete fails by name with what each peer saw.

b2 -a libs/trystero/test/oracle//oracle
b2 -a --dump-tests --out-xml=native.trystero.interop.xml libs/trystero/test/oracle//interop
b2 -a --dump-tests --out-xml=emscripten.trystero.interop.xml toolset=emscripten libs/trystero/test/oracle//interop

The examples over a relay, and their twins

The quick start and each program of the appendix "Differences" (The differences, shown) meet over a Nostr relay of their own, the interop’s test/oracle/interop/relay.mjs on 127.0.0.1, in the lane relayed, natively, which example/Jamfile declares: its driver, example/run_over_relay.mjs, starts the relay, runs the program with the relay’s URL in its environment, TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL, which the program reads, and passes when the program exits with 0 having printed its .expected.

webcpp.drive quick_start : quick_start.cpp
  : <library>/webcpp/trystero//platform <threading>multi : run_over_relay.mjs : : native ;
local differences =
    diff_already_joined
    diff_json_numbers
    diff_json_refused
    diff_passwords
    diff_peer_join
    diff_peers
    diff_relay_config
    diff_relay_sockets
    diff_rooms_per_app
    diff_self_id
    diff_send_to_absent_peer
    ;
for local difference in $(differences)
{
    webcpp.drive $(difference) : $(difference).cpp
      : <library>/webcpp/trystero//platform <threading>multi : run_over_relay.mjs : : native ;
}
webcpp.lane relayed : quick_start $(differences) : native ;
# One needs no relay, its app joining no room, and has no twin.
webcpp.example diff_self_id_not_utf8.cpp
  : <library>/webcpp/trystero//platform <threading>multi : native ;

Each of these programs has its twin in test/oracle/twins/, the same program on Trystero 0.26.0, which the oracle lane runs through test/oracle/run_twin.mjs: a relay of its own, its URL in TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL, and the twin, whose output must be the program’s .expected, or, for a difference, its own .expected, which must differ. The twins agree with 1 of the programs and diverge from 11; 2 have none, each with its reason in test/oracle/twins/without-twin.txt: the chat, a page that prints nothing, and a difference whose original has no counterpart.

Trystero JS has one self id per page, so a twin whose room meets a peer, as a C++ program’s second app does, runs that peer as a second page, a worker thread with Trystero’s modules of its own (test/oracle/page.mjs). Node has no WebRTC: Trystero JS takes werift’s RTCPeerConnection as rtcPolyfill, the WebRTC for Node that Trystero 0.26.0’s own README names, pinned at 0.24.4 in test/oracle/package.json for the twins alone. The C++ programs whose apps meet bind their connections to 127.0.0.1 with stun:127.0.0.1:9, and the twins have no ICE server, so every peer stays on the machine.

b2 -a --dump-tests --out-xml=native.trystero.relayed.xml libs/trystero/example//relayed
b2 -a libs/trystero/test/oracle//twins

The container lanes

Two lanes of the continuous integration, gcc-14 and clang-linux-18, build and run the unit tests with GCC 14 and with clang 18 against libstdc++ in a Linux container, Ubuntu 24.04, with docker run and the network none, which leaves the loopback alone: every test passes, which shows that none reaches beyond the machine (guarantee 6). B2 builds the pinned libsecp256k1, OpenSSL, libdatachannel and nested source dependencies inside the container with the lane’s compiler, runtime and static link configuration. These builds need no network access.

The common OpenSSL provider

The native provider-integration lane builds and runs one application that uses Asio TLS, Beast and Trystero’s platform backend together, natively. It compares the compiled OpenSSL version with the loaded implementation, makes its WebRTC state through trystero’s backend, a peer connection and a data channel, and checks the backend’s relay TLS context, all over the one provider. The run is bounded to 45 seconds and uses the threaded release profile, with exceptions as the build asks. The superproject’s source dependency tests also check that the final Unix executable has no dynamic OpenSSL or libdatachannel provider, that each static archive occurs once and that dependent archives precede OpenSSL in the link order.

The test matrix

The continuous integration runs trystero’s tests in lanes, one toolset each, and its own lanes, the oracle once, the examples over a relay natively, as native.trystero.relayed, and the interop natively and on emscripten, as native.trystero.interop and emscripten.trystero.interop, the release Asyncify tests as emscripten.trystero.asyncify, plus the native provider-integration lane for the common TLS provider. Each lane builds from scratch and records what b2 built and ran; webcpp’s tools/report/report.py merges the files of every lane into a matrix, where each cell says whether that program passed in that lane, or how it failed. The matrix is published with the documentation, at https://webcpporg.github.io/report/.

Reference

Every name trystero declares, in the namespace webcpp::trystero and those nested in it, from the Doc Comments of its headers: each class, function, type and enumerator with its declaration, what it does, what it asks of its caller and how it fails, and the part of Trystero 0.26.0 it ports. The other sections teach the library; this one is where a name is looked up.

The seam between the room and a platform: what a target must provide for a room to run on it. The platform backend provides it on both targets (webcpp/trystero/platform), over webcpp::webrtc, webcpp::beast and webcpp::asio, natively libdatachannel, Boost.Beast and OpenSSL, in a page its own WebRTC, WebSocket and Web Crypto; the tests provide it over memory (test/support).

platform

The platform: one implementation of the backend interface for both targets, over webcpp::webrtc for WebRTC, webcpp::beast for the relays’ WebSockets and webcpp::asio for timers; natively libdatachannel’s WebRTC, Boost.Beast’s WebSockets and OpenSSL’s TLS, AES-GCM and randomness, in a page its own RTCPeerConnection, WebSocket and crypto.subtle. Everything it reports runs on the executor it is given, whose io_context the program runs.

webcpp::trystero::backend

The seam between the room and a platform: what a target must provide for a room to run on it. The platform backend provides it on both targets (webcpp/trystero/platform), over webcpp::webrtc, webcpp::beast and webcpp::asio, natively libdatachannel, Boost.Beast and OpenSSL, in a page its own WebRTC, WebSocket and Web Crypto; the tests provide it over memory (test/support).

Description

Tip: every handler a backend invokes runs on the room’s executor, one at a time, and may destroy the object that invoked it. A backend whose events arrive on other threads (libdatachannel) posts them there first.

Every handler runs after the call that caused it has returned, never inside it: a completion (done) of a peer_connection or a sealer, and a websocket’s close when no socket can be made, are posted even when their result is known at once. The room calls these operations from inside handlers whose state a completion run there would change under them.

Text crosses this interface as std::string_view, valid for the duration of the call or of the handler: a backend reads what it is given before returning, and a handler copies what it keeps. The one exception is a data channel message, handed over by value: the receiver keeps the frame, and taking ownership of it is what spares a copy.

Tip: every method that makes an object takes a memory resource last, the app’s for a peer connection and the room’s for the rest, and the backend allocates the object, its handlers and what it hands to the room (a frame, a text) through it, on the room’s executor only.

Types

Name Description

data_channel

A WebRTC data channel, as the RTCDataChannel a Trystero peer exchanges its frames over.

factory

Makes everything above, and gives a room its randomness and its clocks: one per page in the browser, one per application natively, one per test.

ice_server

A STUN or TURN server, an RTCIceServer of the iceServers Trystero gives RTCPeerConnection.

peer_connection

A WebRTC peer connection, as the RTCPeerConnection of a Trystero peer, whose negotiation the signaling drives: it makes an offer or an answer only when asked to.

sealer

AES-GCM under one room key, in Trystero’s sealed text form (protocol/signal.hpp), what Trystero’s encrypt and decrypt do with crypto.subtle.

timer

A one-shot timer, what the setTimeout calls of Trystero become.

websocket

A WebSocket to a Nostr relay, as the WebSocket Trystero’s relay manager opens.

webcpp::trystero::platform

The platform: one implementation of the backend interface for both targets, over webcpp::webrtc for WebRTC, webcpp::beast for the relays’ WebSockets and webcpp::asio for timers; natively libdatachannel’s WebRTC, Boost.Beast’s WebSockets and OpenSSL’s TLS, AES-GCM and randomness, in a page its own RTCPeerConnection, WebSocket and crypto.subtle. Everything it reports runs on the executor it is given, whose io_context the program runs.

Types

Name Description

backend

The platform’s factory: one per application, beside the executor it runs on, natively or in a page.

backend_config

What a backend makes its peer connections, its relays’ WebSockets and its own state with, beside the app’s app_config::ice_servers.

page_call

A function the page calls into C++ with, made by webcpp::asio’s bridge, each call of which posts f with the value the page passed to the executor’s io_context.

sealer

AES-GCM under one room key, in Trystero’s sealed text form: on emscripten through the page’s crypto.subtle, under a key imported once, as Trystero’s encrypt and decrypt do.

websocket_limits

What a relay’s WebSocket tolerates of a relay that stops reading or answering.

Functions

Name Description

connect_websocket

Connects to a Nostr relay over webcpp::beast, on both targets: ws:// in the clear, wss:// over TLS with tls; natively over Boost.Beast’s own stream, in a page over its WebSocket.

js_string

A JavaScript string of UTF-8 text, decoded straight from the WebAssembly memory the view points into.

make_tls_context

Makes the TLS context of the relays’ wss:// connections, a client of TLS 1.2 or newer that verifies each relay against the system’s certificate authorities.

webcpp::trystero::platform::backend

The platform’s factory: one per application, beside the executor it runs on, natively or in a page.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/platform/backend.hpp>

class backend
    : public trystero::backend::factory

Description

It makes peer connections, data channels and received frames in app_config::memory, and WebSockets, sealers and room timers in the room’s effective room_options::memory; its own state is in backend_config::memory. Objects and their handlers use the resource supplied to their factory method. What libdatachannel and OpenSSL allocate stays theirs, and what emscripten::val holds is in the JavaScript heap.

Its peer connections are webcpp::webrtc’s, counted by a webcpp::webrtc::runtime: its own, or the program’s. Each of its connections and channels keeps its own runtime alive, so that one which outlives the backend, in a handler the io_context still holds, does not outlive the runtime. Natively a process holds one runtime at a time, since libdatachannel’s state is the process’s: a program with several backends at once, or that uses webcpp::webrtc beside trystero, makes one runtime and gives it to each; in a page the census counts the connections of every runtime alike.

Tip: in a page, every object it makes runs on its executor, whose io_context the program runs from main, under a work guard, for as long as the page lives: the page’s events, the timers and the promises it awaits post to that io_context, and run only while it runs. A page needs a secure context (https, or http on localhost), where crypto.subtle exists, for its sealer.

Base Classes

Name Description

trystero::backend::factory

Makes everything above, and gives a room its randomness and its clocks: one per page in the browser, one per application natively, one per test.

Fills out from the platform’s secure source of randomness, natively OpenSSL’s generator, in a page its crypto.getRandomValues; the program aborts when it has none.

runtime

steady_now [virtual]

The standard library’s steady clock, which a page reads from performance.now().

webcpp::trystero::platform::page_call

A function the page calls into C++ with, made by webcpp::asio’s bridge, each call of which posts f with the value the page passed to the executor’s io_context.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/platform/page.hpp>

template<class F>
class page_call final

Description

It is how a page reaches a program whose main runs its io_context: the call returns at once, having run nothing, and f runs when the run family does, never inside the page’s event, in either suspension variant. An embind function would run its work inside the event, and under Asyncify, while main is suspended in its run, returns a promise that never settles, and aborts a debug build at its second call (measured with Emscripten 6.0.11). A call made once the page_call is destroyed, or once its work is posted and the page_call destroyed before it runs, reaches nothing; so does one made once the io_context is destroyed.

f is a handler of the run, and lets no JavaScript error out, webcpp::asio’s rule for every handler: an error that leaves f leaves run with it, and the program’s run never resumes (measured with Emscripten 6.0.11 under node: the process ends with the error, in either suspension variant). A page may pass any value, so f checks its type before it converts it, with isString(), isNumber() or typeOf(), and reads a field only of what is neither null nor undefined: embind’s as<std::string>() of a number throws a BindingError, and a field of undefined a TypeError. A number is read as a double, with as<double>(), and its range checked before it becomes an integer: in a build with assertions, as a debug build is, embind’s as<std::int32_t>() of a number beyond the type’s range, as 1e10, throws a TypeError. f is given the page’s value as it is when f runs, not when the page called: a JavaScript object the page changes meanwhile is seen changed.

webcpp::trystero::platform::sealer

AES-GCM under one room key, in Trystero’s sealed text form: on emscripten through the page’s crypto.subtle, under a key imported once, as Trystero’s encrypt and decrypt do.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/platform/sealer.hpp>

class sealer
    : public backend::sealer
    , public std::enable_shared_from_this<sealer>

Description

Each Web Crypto promise is awaited with webcpp::asio’s browser::async_await, which posts its settlement to the executor, through the io_context’s own executor when the executor is one, so that the wait and the settlement’s post are both in the room’s resource. The text is copied into JavaScript during the call; an operation that arrives while the key is still being imported waits with a copy of its text, in the room’s resource. Without crypto.subtle, outside a secure context, every operation fails. A seal’s IV comes from the platform’s one source of randomness, the page’s crypto.getRandomValues there.

Name Description

How long the connection may stay silent: half of it, a keep-alive ping is sent, and a relay that answers nothing within the whole of it is closed, which reports a close.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/platform/websocket.hpp>

Description

It counts the bytes received, and a ping waits for the write in flight. Native only: a page’s WebSocket cannot ping, so a page’s relay socket has no idle timeout.

webcpp::trystero::platform::websocket_limits::max_queued_bytes

The most bytes of text queued to write: a relay that stops reading lets them pile up, and a text beyond this drops the connection, which reports a close, so that the room reconnects with its backoff.

webcpp::trystero::platform::connect_websocket

Connects to a Nostr relay over webcpp::beast, on both targets: ws:// in the clear, wss:// over TLS with tls; natively over Boost.Beast’s own stream, in a page over its WebSocket.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/platform/websocket.hpp>

std::shared_ptr<backend::websocket>
connect_websocket(
    webcpp::asio::any_io_executor const& ex,
    webcpp::asio::ssl::context* tls,
    std::string_view url,
    backend::websocket::handlers h,
    std::pmr::memory_resource* memory,
    websocket_limits limits = {});

Description

Writes are queued, one in flight at a time; a received text is handed over as a view of the read buffer, a binary message is dropped, and a message longer than protocol::max_relay_message_bytes closes the connection, a page’s before it is copied into WebAssembly, the relay’s first ones too. A relay that stops reading is dropped once the queue, or a page’s bufferedAmount, would pass limits.max_queued_bytes, and, natively, one that stops answering once limits.idle_timeout passes with its keep-alive ping unanswered; each reports one close. The URL is read with Boost.URL: ws:// or wss:// in any case, a host name with its escapes decoded, an IPv4 address as a dotted quad or an IPv6 address in brackets, and a port up to 65535. A URL it refuses, which includes what a page’s URL parser reads otherwise (an IPv4 shorthand such as 127.1, an international name, a tab or a backslash), and a wss:// URL without tls, report a close, as an unreachable relay does. A wss:// connection asks for the relay’s verification whatever the verify mode of tls, on both targets. Natively it names the host to the server (SNI) when it is a name, verifies the relay’s certificate against the authorities of tls, and checks it against the URL’s host, a name or an address; in a page the browser does all three, against its own authorities, and the connection reports a close, making no WebSocket, when tls asks for what a page cannot honour: authorities added, a client certificate or key, options, a method other than tls_client or sslv23_client, or a verify callback other than host_name_verification of the relay’s host. It needs no exceptions.

The connection, its handlers, its queued texts, its read buffer and its operations are in memory. What stays outside it, for each connection: natively what Boost.Beast, Asio and OpenSSL allocate of their own, their streams’ state, the resolver’s, the handshake’s request and response, the verify callback, their timers’ waits, the idle timer’s again at each read, and each keep-alive ping’s frame; a relay that answers the handshake with a status other than 101 has its response’s header read, at most 8 KiB, and no byte of its body, through webcpp::beast’s bounded handshake layer, before the connection reports its close. In a page, for each event of the page’s WebSocket, the open, each message and the close, the C library’s allocation embind makes for its type, and for a message a second, for the type of its data, each freed before the call that made it returns.

Return Value

The WebSocket; destroying it drops the connection without reporting it.

Parameters

Name Description

ex

The executor every handler runs on.

tls

The TLS context of wss://, which must outlive the connection, or null when the program has none; the connection verifies the relay even when its verify mode is verify_none, as Asio makes a client’s context, natively against its authorities and in a page against the browser’s.

url

The relay’s URL, read during the call.

h

What the WebSocket reports.

memory

The room’s resource, which the connection’s own allocations are in.

limits

What it tolerates of a relay that stops reading or answering.

See Also

"The platform backend", in the guide.

"What stays outside the resource", in the guide.

webcpp::trystero::platform::make_tls_context

Makes the TLS context of the relays’ wss:// connections, a client of TLS 1.2 or newer that verifies each relay against the system’s certificate authorities.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/platform/websocket.hpp>

[[nodiscard]]
boost::system::result<webcpp::asio::ssl::context>
make_tls_context();

Description

Natively the authorities are those OpenSSL’s default verify paths name, the system’s own; a relay whose certificate does not verify is unreachable. On Windows those paths are in OpenSSL’s build-time directory, which neither Windows nor webcpp fills, and OpenSSL reads no Windows certificate store by default, so there are none there unless SSL_CERT_FILE or SSL_CERT_DIR names some: a Windows program gives the backend its own context. A program that trusts other authorities, as webcpp’s embedded Mozilla roots (webcpp::asio::make_tls_client_context()) or a private one, makes its context itself and gives it to the backend. In the browser the page’s WebSocket verifies the relay against the browser’s authorities, and the context records only the policy its stream asks for: a client that verifies its peer.

Return Value

The context, or the error that kept OpenSSL from making it or from finding the system’s authorities.

Note

The return value should not be discarded.

See Also

"The relays", in the guide.

webcpp::trystero::protocol

Namespaces

Name Description

json

Reading and writing the protocol’s JSON texts on webcpp::document, with every value in the resource the caller gives. A text is read by webcpp::document::parse into a webcpp::document::pmr::document of that resource, whose image and working state are allocated there; a text the protocol writes is a fixed shape of a few strings and numbers, so it is appended field by field, its strings quoted as JSON.stringify quotes them, rather than built as a document, which would copy every string into a node of its own before writing it again.

webcpp::trystero::protocol::json

Reading and writing the protocol’s JSON texts on webcpp::document, with every value in the resource the caller gives. A text is read by webcpp::document::parse into a webcpp::document::pmr::document of that resource, whose image and working state are allocated there; a text the protocol writes is a fixed shape of a few strings and numbers, so it is appended field by field, its strings quoted as JSON.stringify quotes them, rather than built as a document, which would copy every string into a node of its own before writing it again.

webcpp::trystero::protocol::json::protocol_limits

The limits of a protocol text’s parse: at most max_bytes of text, nested at most max_protocol_depth deep, into an image that grows to at most twice that and 64 KiB more.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/protocol/json.hpp>

constexpr
webcpp::document::parse_options
protocol_limits(uint64_t max_bytes) noexcept;

Description

Tip: a text Trystero writes holds a few dozen values at most, each node some 200 bytes of image beside its string, so the image of the longest is under its text and 16 KiB. A text that needs more holds thousands of values, which no Trystero message has; it is refused once its image has grown to the bound, so that no text costs a room more than a multiple of its bound to read. The depth bounds what the parse’s recursion takes of the stack, far below document’s 256.

Return Value

The options.

Parameters

Name Description

max_bytes

The longest text the caller reads.

webcpp::trystero::protocol::nostr

Types

Name Description

closed

A relay’s ["CLOSED", <subscription>, <reason>]: the relay ended a subscription.

eose

A relay’s ["EOSE", <subscription>]: the stored events of a subscription were all sent.

event

A relay’s ["EVENT", <subscription>, <event>]: an event of a subscription, as views.

notice

A relay’s ["NOTICE", <text>]: a message for humans.

ok

A relay’s ["OK", <id>, <accepted>, <reason>]: whether it took a published event, as views.

signer

A BIP-340 key pair over libsecp256k1, the one key a peer signs every event with, as Trystero’s Nostr strategy does with its pubkey.

webcpp::trystero::protocol::nostr::has_own_id

Whether an event’s id is its own, the SHA-256 of NIP-01’s serialization of the event [0,<pubkey>,<created_at>,<kind>,<tags>,<content>], which event_id computes.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/protocol/nostr.hpp>

bool
has_own_id(
    event const& e,
    std::pmr::memory_resource* memory = std::pmr::get_default_resource());

Description

A relay sends whatever id it chooses, so an id that is not its event’s own may be another event’s. Only an event whose one tag is its topic’s and whose public key is 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits is checked, as Trystero writes every event; any other has no id of its own here, whatever it says.

Return Value

Whether the id is the hexadecimal of the SHA-256 of the event’s serialization.

Parameters

Name Description

e

The event, as read_relay_message reads it.

memory

The resource the escaped topic and content are allocated in, during the call.

webcpp::trystero::protocol::nostr::max_parsed_relay_text_bytes

The longest text of a relay a room reads, in bytes: a longer one is dropped before it is read, and the connection goes on; one longer than max_relay_message_bytes closes the connection instead.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/protocol/nostr.hpp>

inline constexpr std::size_t max_parsed_relay_text_bytes = max_parsed_signal_bytes + 2048;

Description

The longest text measured is an event that carries an answer, 1,244 bytes, among Trystero JS in Chrome and both backends. The bound is an event that carries the longest signal a room reads (max_parsed_signal_bytes), with 2 KiB for the event’s other fields, the subscription id and the escaping of the signal’s quotes, which take some 600 bytes.

webcpp::trystero::protocol::frame_kind

The kind of an action frame, the low four bits of its second byte, in Trystero’s action wire, version 2.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/protocol/action_wire.hpp>

enum class frame_kind : uint8_t;

Description

A payload that fits one frame travels inline; a larger one is offered, accepted by the receiver, then sent in chunks. Integers and float64 values are big-endian, as DataView writes them.

| Frame | Bytes | | inline (kind 0) | 2, kind or format << 4, name (32 bytes, NUL padded), metadata length | | | (uint16), metadata, payload | | offer (kind 1) | the inline header, transfer id (uint32), payload size (float64), | | | metadata | | chunk (kind 2) | 2, 2, transfer id (uint32), offset (float64), bytes | | accepted (kind 3) | 2, 3, transfer id (uint32) | | rejected (kind 4) | 2, 4, transfer id (uint32), reason (UTF-8, at most 200 bytes) | | cancelled (kind 5) | 2, 5, transfer id (uint32) |

chunk

A piece of a transfer’s payload, Trystero’s chunk.

accepted

The receiver accepts an offer, Trystero’s accepted.

rejected

The receiver refuses an offer, Trystero’s rejected.

cancelled

The sender gives a transfer up, Trystero’s cancelled.

webcpp::trystero::protocol::random_id

An id of one character of id_alphabet for each random byte, Trystero’s genId.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/protocol/topics.hpp>

std::pmr::string
random_id(
    std::span<uint8_t const> random,
    std::pmr::memory_resource* memory = std::pmr::get_default_resource());

Description

Each byte picks the character at its remainder in 62, as Trystero picks one character of its charSet for each draw, so an id of n characters takes n random bytes.

Tip: 256 is not a multiple of 62, so each of the first eight characters comes from 5 of the 256 bytes and each other from 4, where Trystero draws each of the 62 alike: a character carries about 5.95 bits of its byte’s 8, a little less than log2(62).

Return Value

The id, as long as random.

Parameters

Name Description

random

The random bytes, one for each character.

memory

The resource the id is allocated in.

Description

The longest signal measured is an answer, 762 bytes, among Trystero JS in Chrome and both backends, which trickle their candidates. The bound is the longest signal the bounds of its fields admit, a sealed offer or answer of max_sealed_description_bytes with the longest ids, and 1 KiB to spare, so that it refuses no signal they accept.

webcpp::trystero::webrtc

The backend’s WebRTC over webcpp::webrtc, the same on both targets: natively libdatachannel’s, in the browser the page’s own. The platform backend makes its peer connections here, and what remains of the platform is webcpp::webrtc’s.

webcpp::trystero::webrtc::data_channel

A data channel over webcpp::webrtc’s, the backend’s RTCDataChannel, which carries a peer’s frames.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/webrtc/data_channel.hpp>

class data_channel
    : public backend::data_channel
    , public std::enable_shared_from_this<data_channel>

Description

It reads every message as it comes, with async_receive, on the executor. A text message, as a peer can send, or a binary one larger than any room frame (protocol::max_room_frame_bytes), is then dropped: neither can be a frame. Frames received while no message handler is installed wait in the app’s resource, in order, up to max_pending_frames for pending_frames_ttl from the first, Trystero’s pending-data bounds; exceeding either closes the channel. Installing a receiver posts their delivery, so that set_handlers never calls it inline. In the browser, a message larger than webcpp::webrtc’s options::max_message_size, or past its receive budget, closes the channel too.

Tip: a received frame is read once, by webcpp::webrtc, into a vector of the app’s resource, which the message handler then owns; what the platform holds before is the platform’s.

webcpp::trystero::webrtc::peer_connection

A peer connection over webcpp::webrtc’s, the backend’s RTCPeerConnection, with its negotiation driven by the signaling: an offer or an answer exists only when set_local_description asks for one.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/webrtc/peer_connection.hpp>

class peer_connection
    : public backend::peer_connection
    , public std::enable_shared_from_this<peer_connection>

Description

It keeps a wait of each kind pending on its connection, re-armed on the executor, and reports through the handlers what each completes with:

| webcpp::webrtc | Reported | | async_wait_ice_candidate | the JSON of an RTCIceCandidateInit | | async_wait_state_change, and the ICE state’s wait | one state, merging both | | async_accept_data_channel | the channel, as a data_channel |

The merged state is the browser’s view of both: failed when either failed, then closed, disconnected, connected (or ICE completed), connecting (or ICE checking), and new.

Tip: the connection, its channels, its handlers, its operations and the texts it hands to the app are in the app’s resource; what the platform holds (libdatachannel’s objects, or the page’s) is the platform’s.

    std::span<backend::ice_server const> servers,
    std::string_view bind_address,
    backend::factory& factory,
    std::pmr::memory_resource* memory);

Description

A connection that is not bound gathers a host candidate on each interface but the loopback, which ICE never offers (RFC 8445, 5.1.1.1); natively, one bound to an address, as "127.0.0.1", gathers on that address alone, which lets two peers of one machine connect with no other network. The browser cannot honour it.

Return Value

The connection, or webcpp::webrtc’s error: too_many_peer_connections past the runtime’s cap, syntax_error for an ICE server URL the platform cannot parse, operation_error for another refusal.

Note

The return value should not be discarded.

Parameters

Name Description

runtime

The runtime that counts the connection, which it keeps alive.

ex

The executor every handler of the connection runs on.

servers

The STUN and TURN servers it gathers through, read during the call.

bind_address

The local address it binds to, natively; empty for every interface.

factory

The backend, which makes its channels’ timers, and which outlives every operation of the connection.

memory

The app’s resource: the connection, its channels, its handlers and its texts are allocated in it.

webcpp::trystero::action::async_send

Sends a message to options.targets, or every active peer, Trystero’s send.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/room.hpp>

template<class CompletionToken>
auto
async_send(
    T value,
    send_options options,
    CompletionToken&& token);

Description

A payload that fits one frame is sent inline; a larger one is offered, accepted by each receiver, and sent in chunks. Completes with (error_code) once each target’s local data channel has taken the inline frame, or the last chunk of a transfer the receiver accepted, as Trystero’s send resolves: nothing confirms that the receiver has the message. It completes with the first failure: error::invalid_action_name, error::metadata_too_large, error::no_such_peer, error::transfer_rejected, error::transfer_timed_out, error::channel_stalled, error::peer_disconnected or error::room_left.

Return Value

What the token’s initiation returns.

Template Parameters

CompletionToken

An Asio completion token for void(error_code).

value

The message, taken at the call: moved when T owns its storage, copied once into the room’s resource when it is a view, and serialized at once into the room’s resource when it is a JSON document, or a payload that holds one.

The targets and the metadata.

The completion token.

Description

webcpp::trystero::app_config::memory

The resource every allocation of the app goes through: its state, its connections, the peer connections and data channels its rooms’ negotiations make, the frames received on them, the sentences of its log; not null.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/options.hpp>

std::pmr::memory_resource* memory = std::pmr::get_default_resource();

Description

What libdatachannel, OpenSSL and the browser’s JavaScript allocate stays theirs. The app uses the resource from its executor only, so it need not be thread-safe when that executor runs on one thread. It must outlive the app, its rooms, retained values allocated in it and every operation they leave pending: on Asio, until the io_context their executor belongs to has run out of their work or has been destroyed, so a resource is declared before its io_context; in the browser, until the app’s and its rooms’ pending promises have settled. The app and its rooms allocate and free per event, so a resource that reuses what is freed (a pool) suits a long-lived app, and a monotonic one only a short-lived one.

See Also

"Allocation", in the guide.

webcpp::trystero::app_config::password

The password shared by every room of this app, Trystero’s password.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/options.hpp>

std::pmr::string password = = {};

Description

The app copies it into its resource and keeps it unchanged. Different passwords require separate apps with distinct peer ids, so a connection authenticated in one domain cannot be reused in another. Empty means a passwordless domain. Signals are still sealed with the app and room ids, and the room handshake then has no password challenge.

A move-only callable of the signature R(Args...), which holds its target inline when the target fits in three pointers and is nothrow-movable, and otherwise in storage of its allocator.

    class R,

Description

It replaces std::function wherever trystero keeps a handler, including the backend, app, rooms and log sink, since std::function takes no allocator since C++17. Each handler uses its owner’s std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<>, over app_config::memory or the effective room_options::memory; one constructed from a callable alone uses the default resource. The resource must outlive the handler.

Tip: a move assignment carries the source’s allocator with its target, as moving the target there does; the allocator-extended move, which a std::pmr container uses, moves the target into another resource when the two differ.

webcpp::trystero::room

A room joined over Trystero’s Nostr strategy, what Trystero’s joinRoom returns.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/room.hpp>

class room;

Description

app::join makes it, joined; async_leave leaves with Trystero’s farewell, and destroying it leaves at once. Its peers meet over the relays, connect over WebRTC through the connections its app shares between its rooms, and exchange the messages of the actions it makes, wire compatible with Trystero’s JavaScript.

Every room uses its app’s immutable password. Initial sealed signaling authenticates that domain before a connection is adopted. The unchanged JS room handshake verifies only at the lower id; different passwords require separate apps with distinct self ids.

Tip: every handler the room calls, and every completion, runs on its app’s executor. The views a handler receives are valid for the duration of the call. Every allocation of the room goes through its effective room_options::memory, the app’s resource when null; shared connections and received frames use app_config::memory. A completion handler is allocated as its own associated allocator says. Destroying the room leaves operations pending on its executor, so both resources must outlive those operations and every retained value allocated in them.

webcpp::trystero::room::on_error

Sets what is called with each problem with one peer that the room handled itself, as a wrong password or a timed-out handshake, Trystero’s onPeerError.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/room.hpp>

template<class F>
requires std::is_invocable_v<F&, std::string_view, boost::system::error_code,
                                     std::string_view>
void
on_error(F&& f);

Description

Signals that do not open with the room key (error::wrong_password) are reported once per negotiation, and paced: the first of a quiet 10 s at once, with its peer, and the others of those 10 s in one report, with an empty peer id and a description that starts with their number, since anyone who reads the relays can send them from any number of fresh ids. A part of the configuration the app set aside is reported to app::on_error, not here.

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/options.hpp>

webcpp::trystero::error

What an operation of the library completes with when it does not succeed.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/error.hpp>

enum class error : int;

Description

Each value is one of the errors Trystero rejects a promise with or reports to onPeerError, as a code of error_category rather than a message: an operation completes with it, and room::on_error reports it with the peer it concerns.

Members

Name Description

room_left

The room was left while the operation was pending, Trystero’s "room left".

no_such_peer

The target is not an active peer of the room, Trystero’s "no active peer with id".

peer_disconnected

The peer went away before the operation finished, Trystero’s "peer disconnected".

invalid_action_name

The action’s name is not 1 to 32 UTF-8 bytes without NUL, as Trystero requires.

metadata_too_large

The action’s metadata does not fit one frame, Trystero’s "action metadata is too large".

transfer_rejected

The receiver refused a transfer, or a received payload is not of the awaited type.

transfer_timed_out

The receiver neither accepted nor refused a transfer in time.

channel_stalled

The data channel stopped draining while a transfer waited for it.

wrong_password

A peer’s signal or handshake used another password, or the peer sent a handshake message the protocol does not expect, Trystero’s "incorrect password for overlapping room".

handshake_timed_out

A connected peer did not finish the handshake in time, Trystero’s "handshake timed out".

handshake_failed

Reserved: nothing reports it today.

backend_failure

The browser or the native stack refused an operation.

invalid_configuration

The app’s configuration holds something it cannot use, as an ICE server whose URL WebRTC refuses; the app goes on without it, and app::on_error reports it with no peer.

already_joined

The app already holds a room of that id; a room is joined once per app.

too_many_rooms

The app already holds as many rooms as a peer accepts, 64 of them.

See Also

"Rooms and actions", in the guide.

WEBCPP_TRYSTERO_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Defined when trystero is built without exceptions: when webcpp has none (the compiler has none, or the developer defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS for every webcpp library), or when the developer defines it alone, to disable trystero’s in a build that has them.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/trystero/config.hpp>

#define WEBCPP_TRYSTERO_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Description

trystero raises no exception of its own: every operation that can fail completes with an error code, and every part of it, the platform backend included, works with exceptions and without them. Its WebRTC is webcpp::webrtc’s, which natively calls libdatachannel’s C API, where no exception crosses.

See Also

"The platform backend", in the guide.

Appendix A: Differences from Trystero

trystero ports the part of Trystero 0.26.0 that rooms of messages need: the Nostr strategy, the signaling, the password handshake, the action wire and the room’s API. Where it keeps a feature, it keeps Trystero’s wire and its defaults; where it bounds what a peer or a relay can make a room hold, it says so in Bounded signaling, since Trystero JS bounds none of it. These features of Trystero are not ported, each for its reason:

Not ported Why

Audio and video: addStream, removeStream, addTrack, removeTrack, replaceTrack, onPeerStream and onPeerTrack, with the actions @_stream, @_track and @_signal and their renegotiation

The largest part left, on the roadmap (Roadmap): in the browser, the page’s MediaStream objects; natively, libdatachannel’s RTP tracks, whose capture, encoding and decoding would be the application’s. A room ignores a frame of one of these actions.

Request actions, kind: 'request': request, requestMany and onRequest

Not ported yet: an application answers a message with another, to its sender’s id.

onReceive, which accepts or declines an incoming transfer; the progress callbacks onProgress and onReceiveProgress; and cancelling a send with an AbortSignal

Not ported yet: a room accepts every transfer for an action with a receiver within max_receive_bytes, as Trystero does when no onReceive is set, and reports a transfer only when it completes.

onPeerHandshake, a handshake of the application’s own

Not ported yet: the password handshake, which runs on the same internal action, @_hsdata, is.

Passive rooms, passive: true

Not ported yet: a room always announces itself.

The BitTorrent, MQTT, Firebase, Supabase, IPFS and WebSocket relay strategies

Each is a strategy of its own to port; Nostr’s public relays need no account and no server of the application’s own.

getRelaySockets, pauseRelayReconnection, resumeRelayReconnection, manualReconnection and warnOnRelayFailure

Not ported yet: a room reconnects with its backoff, and reports what its relays do through its log.

trickleIce: false, turnConfig and rtcPolyfill

Candidates are always trickled, as Trystero’s Nostr strategy does by default; ice_servers names every STUN and TURN server, in place of Trystero’s defaults; and the backend is what a polyfill would be.

A feature not ported has no program among the differences below: trystero has nothing of it to run beside its twin.

Where a ported feature behaves otherwise

Behaviour Trystero JS Here Why

Scope of sharing and of the self id

the page: one selfId for every app and room, one manager per strategy

an app object: its self id and its connections

no static state; several peers in one process; an id across apps is a program’s choice (app_config::self_id) and never reaches the wire of another app

Passwords across rooms

independently configured per room, including mixed passwords on one shared connection

one immutable app_config::password for every room, separate apps and self ids for different passwords

the initial sealed negotiation authenticates one password domain before any of its rooms reuse the connection; the JS wire remains unchanged

A peer kicked from a room, or that kicked us, over a live connection

bound again by its next signal or presence

bound again at a rebinding time, 11 s doubling to 5 min; the lower id refuses it meanwhile and keeps its frames

a peer sending invalid room proofs would otherwise loop reports and announcements without end; one refusing side cannot alternate with another

Reuse over a live connection

binds on any signal of that peer id

binds only a peer that advertised the room’s token itself, and by reuse only on their first meeting over that connection

a forged announcement must not bind an innocent peer

A room frame before the peer’s presence for the room

kept until the room binds by presence or by reuse

also taken as the peer’s advertisement of the room, which binds it

a forged announcement cannot reuse, so a presence that Chrome dropped as the page’s channel opened would otherwise leave the room unbound for good; only the peer writes its connection’s frames

Announcements after a peer leaves

restarted after every leave

restarted only when no live connection to that peer remains

over a live connection, rebinding goes through the connection

Presence after binding

sent when a room registers

also sent again when a room binds by reuse or at its rebinding time

it makes the other side, Trystero JS included, bind at once

An answer to an earlier challenge

checked against the current challenge only

accepted when it is correct for any of the last 8 challenges sent since the last completed handshake

a late answer of an ended binding is honest and proves the password; failing it reports a false error

Frames after the higher id’s own kick

kept for the next binding

dropped until the higher id sends presence

they belong to the ended binding; flushed into the next one, they would answer or be answered in its place

the same room

unbounded; a peer advertising a 65th is dropped by the other side

the 65th would cost every connection of the app

A connection whose last room was kicked

idle 123,333 ms

closed at once

a bound: a failed peer holds no connection

Relay sockets and the Nostr key

shared by the rooms of the page, topics batched per socket

per room

not part of this decision; invisible to peers; shared through the app in a later change

Relay and ICE configuration

the first room’s relays; each negotiating room’s RTC configuration

the app’s, for every room

one configuration for what the rooms share

idle_timeout

test-only (_test_only_sharedPeerIdleMs)

a configuration member, Trystero’s default

tests and programs that close sooner

Frames waiting for a bound room’s handler

64, 10 s, then the connection drops

no such state

a binding’s delivery is set when it is made

Renegotiation and media over a shared connection

routed through a control room, streams owned per room; a connection with any media is destroyed when its last room goes

not ported

media is on the roadmap (Roadmap)

Passive rooms

presence only for active rooms

not ported

not ported yet: a room always announces itself

Duplicate connections

the first registered wins at each side and the other is closed at once; crossed, both lose and meet again

the first registered wins at each side; the other is held, unused, until the peer shows which it keeps: closed once the peer sends on the first, or after 2 s (higher id) or 10 s (lower id) when the peer does neither; it replaces the first when the peer closes the first, or, for the higher id, when the peer sends on it

libdatachannel ends an association with a stream reset and a SHUTDOWN, its ABORT a moment later, where a browser’s ABORT follows its reset at once: closing at once the connection a Trystero JS peer kept, as it starts sending on it, made Chrome fail those sends and Trystero JS report a peer error. Following the peer’s choice closes no connection the peer uses, keeps a crossed pair’s rooms on the connection the peer kept, and still agrees with Trystero’s rule

A Nostr event a relay repeats, or that several relays carry

acted on each time

acted on once among the 4096 newest event ids, when its id is checked to be its own, the SHA-256 of its NIP-01 serialization; an event with any other id is acted on each time and its id never kept

every relay of the room carries each event; an id taken unchecked would let a relay hide a genuine event behind a forged one it sends first under the same id, or fill the room’s resource with the ids kept

A relay’s text, a signal or a handshake message past its bound

parsed with JSON.parse whatever its length, under the relay’s own limit

dropped before it is read: 68,608 bytes for a relay’s text, 66,560 for a signal, 1,024 for a handshake message (JSON texts)

the bounds are those of the fields Trystero sends, so no text a Trystero peer writes is refused; a longer one would cost the room its length to read

A protocol text of thousands of values

parsed

refused once its image passes twice its bound and 64 KiB

no Trystero message holds more than a few dozen values, and a document’s value takes some 200 bytes of image

A protocol text nested deeper than 16

parsed

dropped as a malformed one is

no Trystero message nests deeper than 4, a relay’s event and its tags, and each level of a parse is a level of recursion, which a hostile relay would otherwise take to 256

A self id that is not UTF-8

impossible: a JavaScript string

set aside for a random one, with a configuration report

JSON carries UTF-8 alone, and a signal writes the id as a JSON string

A JSON payload’s number that a double cannot hold: an integer past 253, a decimal of more digits, one past a double’s range

sent as the nearest double, and one past a double’s range as null: a JavaScript number is a double

sent exact, as webcpp::document holds it; a Trystero JS peer reads the nearest double, or Infinity

webcpp::document keeps every number exact, and writes each one a double holds as JavaScript does

A JSON payload nested deeper than 256, or holding a lone surrogate

delivered: JSON.parse takes both

not delivered

webcpp::document’s defaults: a bounded depth, and strings that are UTF-8

A JSON payload whose document passes the room’s room_options::max_json_document_bytes, 64 MiB by default: some 350,000 values of one character

delivered: JSON.parse has no bound but the page’s memory

not delivered (A JSON payload nested deeper than 256, holding a lone surrogate, or past the room’s bound)

each value of a document is a node of 192 bytes of image, 96 times its text at most, so a program bounds what a peer’s JSON may take of its room’s resource; every payload within the bound is delivered

The characters of a random id (the self id, offer ids, nonces, subscription ids)

each of the 62 alike, from Math.random

one random byte each, at its remainder in 62: each of the first eight characters from 5 of the 256 bytes, each other from 4, about 5.95 bits a character

the bytes come from the backend’s secure randomness, not Math.random; the bias costs about 0.005 bits a character, below log2(62)

Each difference a program can show has one, example/diff_<topic>.cpp, with its twin, the same program on Trystero 0.26.0, in test/oracle/twins/ (The differences, shown); The differences no program shows gives the reason of each other row.

The differences, shown

Each difference below is shown by a C++ program and, but for the last, its twin, the same program written for Trystero JS: the part of the C++ program that differs, the twin whole, then what the twin printed on Trystero 0.26.0, then what the C++ program printed. Both ran, and the outputs are theirs: a program and its twin each join over a Nostr relay of their own on 127.0.0.1, whose URL is in their environment, TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL, and two peers of one program meet there, as two apps in C++ and as two pages in Trystero JS (The examples over a relay, and their twins). The lane relayed runs the programs again, and the oracle lane the twins, and each fails when its program no longer prints what is shown here. The twins of the programs of example/ agree with 1 of them, the quick start among them (Quick start), and diverge from 11, each a difference below; 2 programs have no twin, the last difference below and the chat page, each with its reason in test/oracle/twins/without-twin.txt.

Joining a room already joined

Trystero JS

joinRoom with the id of a room the page holds returns that room.

trystero

app::join refuses with error::already_joined while a room of that id is joined.

Why

A room is a handle whose destruction leaves the room: two handles of one room would leave it twice.

trystero::app app(io.get_executor(), backend,
                  {.app_id = "webcpp-trystero-differences", .relay_urls = {relay}});
auto first = app.join("lobby");
const auto second = app.join("lobby");
std::cout << "the first join: " << (first ? std::string("a room") : first.error().message())
          << '\n'
          << "the second join: "
          << (second ? std::string("another room") : second.error().message()) << '\n';
The twin, on Trystero JS
import {joinRoom} from 'trystero'

const config = {appId: 'webcpp-trystero-differences', relayConfig: {urls: [process.env.TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL]}}
const first = joinRoom(config, 'lobby')
const second = joinRoom(config, 'lobby')
console.log('the first join: a room')
console.log(`the second join: ${second === first ? 'the room of the first join' : 'another room'}`)
await first.leave()
Trystero JS prints
the first join: a room
the second join: the room of the first join
trystero prints
the first join: a room
the second join: the app has already joined a room of that id

Rooms per app

Trystero JS

joinRoom joins every room a page asks for: the 65th, 66th and 67th rooms of one appId are each a room. It advertises every room of the app over every connection of the app, and a peer that is advertised a 65th room token over one connection drops that connection, "too many advertised rooms" (dist/shared-peer.mjs:457).

trystero

app::join refuses a 65th room with error::too_many_rooms. A room still in its farewell, the 99 ms of async_leave, counts, so another room can be joined once that leave has completed.

Why

A 65th room would be advertised over every connection of the app, and each Trystero JS peer at the other end would drop the connection.

for (std::size_t n = 1; n <= 64; ++n) {
    join("room-" + std::to_string(n));
}
std::cout << "joins 1 to 64: " << rooms.size() << " rooms\n";
std::cout << "join 65: " << join("room-65") << '\n';
rooms.front().async_leave([&](boost::system::error_code) {
    std::cout << "join 67, once room 1 has left: " << join("room-67") << '\n';
    leave_all();
});
std::cout << "join 66, while room 1 is leaving: " << join("room-66") << '\n';
The twin, on Trystero JS
import {joinRoom} from 'trystero'

const config = {appId: 'webcpp-trystero-differences', relayConfig: {urls: [process.env.TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL]}}
const rooms = []
// What a join gives, a room kept until the end or the error that refused it.
const join = roomId => {
    try {
        rooms.push(joinRoom(config, roomId))
        return 'a room'
    } catch (error) {
        return error.message
    }
}
// tag::example[]
for (let n = 1; n <= 64; ++n) join(`room-${n}`)
console.log(`joins 1 to 64: ${rooms.length} rooms`)
console.log(`join 65: ${join('room-65')}`)
const leaving = rooms[0].leave()
console.log(`join 66, while room 1 is leaving: ${join('room-66')}`)
await leaving
console.log(`join 67, once room 1 has left: ${join('room-67')}`)
// end::example[]
await Promise.all(rooms.slice(1).map(room => room.leave()))
Trystero JS prints
joins 1 to 64: 64 rooms
join 65: a room
join 66, while room 1 is leaving: a room
join 67, once room 1 has left: a room
trystero prints
joins 1 to 64: 64 rooms
join 65: the app holds as many rooms as a peer accepts, 64
join 66, while room 1 is leaving: the app holds as many rooms as a peer accepts, 64
join 67, once room 1 has left: a room

The self id

Trystero JS

A page has one selfId, drawn once when Trystero’s module loads, and every room of every app announces it, so a peer that meets the page in two apps sees the same id in both. Its one manager of shared connections keys them by app id, so the two apps share the id and not their connections.

trystero

Each app draws its own self id and holds its own connections, so a peer that meets the program in rooms of two apps sees two ids, and two rooms of one app show one. A program that wants one id across apps names it, app_config::self_id.

Why

No static state, so that one process holds several peers; an id shared across apps is the program’s choice, and never reaches another app’s wire unless the program chooses it.

// Each app draws a self id of its own, unless app_config::self_id names one for both.
trystero::app first(io.get_executor(), backend, config(first_app));
trystero::app second(io.get_executor(), backend, config(second_app));
auto lobby = first.join("lobby");
auto kitchen = first.join("kitchen");
auto second_lobby = second.join("lobby");
// What the other peer meets in those three rooms.
const auto report = [](std::string_view in_lobby, std::string_view in_kitchen,
                       std::string_view in_second_lobby) {
    std::cout << "two rooms of one app: " << (in_lobby == in_kitchen ? "one id" : "two ids")
              << '\n'
              << "rooms of two apps: " << (in_lobby == in_second_lobby ? "one id" : "two ids")
              << '\n';
};
The twin, on Trystero JS
import {joinRoom} from 'trystero'
import {RTCPeerConnection} from 'werift'
import {openPage} from '../page.mjs'

// The peers meet on this machine alone: no ICE server, werift's WebRTC for Node.
const config = {
    relayConfig: {urls: [process.env.TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL]},
    rtcConfig: {iceServers: []},
}
const firstApp = 'webcpp-trystero-differences'
const secondApp = 'webcpp-trystero-differences-second'
// The other peer, another page, in the rooms this page joins: it posts the id it meets first in
// each.
const other = openPage(async ({joinRoom, RTCPeerConnection, data, post, next}) => {
    const {config, firstApp, secondApp} = data
    const join = (appId, roomId) => joinRoom({...config, appId, rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}, roomId)
    const rooms = [join(firstApp, 'lobby'), join(firstApp, 'kitchen'), join(secondApp, 'lobby')]
    post(await Promise.all(rooms.map(room => new Promise(met => (room.onPeerJoin = met)))))
    await next()
    await Promise.all(rooms.map(room => room.leave()))
}, {config, firstApp, secondApp})

// tag::example[]
// Every room of the page announces the page's selfId, which Trystero draws once, as it loads.
const join = (appId, roomId) => joinRoom({...config, appId, rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}, roomId)
const rooms = [join(firstApp, 'lobby'), join(firstApp, 'kitchen'), join(secondApp, 'lobby')]
// What the other peer meets in those three rooms.
const [inLobby, inKitchen, inSecondLobby] = await other.next()
console.log(`two rooms of one app: ${inLobby === inKitchen ? 'one id' : 'two ids'}`)
console.log(`rooms of two apps: ${inLobby === inSecondLobby ? 'one id' : 'two ids'}`)
// end::example[]
other.post('leave')
await Promise.all([...rooms.map(room => room.leave()), other.done])
Trystero JS prints
two rooms of one app: one id
rooms of two apps: one id
trystero prints
two rooms of one app: one id
rooms of two apps: two ids

Passwords across rooms

Trystero JS

Each joinRoom takes its own password, so one page joins a lobby with one password and a kitchen with another, and a peer that joins both meets the page as one peer, over one connection that carries both rooms’ password handshakes.

trystero

A password is an app’s, app_config::password, the same for every room of the app and never changed: rooms of different passwords are rooms of separate apps, each with its own self id and connections, so the other peer meets two peers.

Why

The sealed negotiation that makes a connection authenticates one password before any room of the app reuses it; the wire stays Trystero’s.

// A password is an app's: a room with another password is a room of another app.
trystero::app one(io.get_executor(), backend, config("one"));
trystero::app two(io.get_executor(), backend, config("two"));
auto lobby = one.join("lobby");
auto kitchen = two.join("kitchen");
// What the two rooms meet.
const auto report = [](std::string_view in_lobby, std::string_view in_kitchen) {
    std::cout << "the lobby, with the password \"one\": joined\n"
              << "the kitchen, with the password \"two\": joined\n"
              << "the peer in both rooms: "
              << (in_lobby == in_kitchen ? "one peer" : "two peers") << '\n';
};
The twin, on Trystero JS
import {joinRoom} from 'trystero'
import {RTCPeerConnection} from 'werift'
import {openPage} from '../page.mjs'

// The peers meet on this machine alone: no ICE server, werift's WebRTC for Node.
const config = {
    appId: 'webcpp-trystero-differences',
    relayConfig: {urls: [process.env.TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL]},
    rtcConfig: {iceServers: []},
}
// The other peer, another page, with the same passwords for the same rooms.
const other = openPage(async ({joinRoom, RTCPeerConnection, data, next}) => {
    const lobby = joinRoom({...data, password: 'one', rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}, 'lobby')
    const kitchen = joinRoom({...data, password: 'two', rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}, 'kitchen')
    await next()
    await Promise.all([lobby.leave(), kitchen.leave()])
}, config)

// tag::example[]
// A password is a room's: one page joins rooms of different passwords.
const lobby = joinRoom({...config, password: 'one', rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}, 'lobby')
const kitchen = joinRoom({...config, password: 'two', rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}, 'kitchen')
// What the two rooms meet.
const met = room => new Promise(joined => (room.onPeerJoin = joined))
const [inLobby, inKitchen] = await Promise.all([met(lobby), met(kitchen)])
console.log('the lobby, with the password "one": joined')
console.log('the kitchen, with the password "two": joined')
console.log(`the peer in both rooms: ${inLobby === inKitchen ? 'one peer' : 'two peers'}`)
// end::example[]
other.post('leave')
await Promise.all([lobby.leave(), kitchen.leave(), other.done])
Trystero JS prints
the lobby, with the password "one": joined
the kitchen, with the password "two": joined
the peer in both rooms: one peer
trystero prints
the lobby, with the password "one": joined
the kitchen, with the password "two": joined
the peer in both rooms: two peers

Relay and ICE configuration

Trystero JS

The first room a page joins, while it holds no other, opens the relays, and every room joined while one remains uses them, whatever relays it was given. A connection is made with the RTC configuration of the room that negotiates it, and a room that binds over it later shares it. So a kitchen joined with a second configuration after the lobby uses the lobby’s relays and the lobby’s ICE servers.

trystero

Relays and ICE servers are the app’s, for every room of the app: a room with another configuration is a room of another app, which uses its own. A room hands out neither its relays’ sockets nor its connections, so the program gives each app a backend that records what the app asks of the platform’s.

Why

One configuration for what the rooms of an app share.

// A configuration is an app's: the kitchen, joined with the second, is a room of a second app.
trystero::app lobby_app(io.get_executor(), first_backend, config(first));
trystero::app kitchen_app(io.get_executor(), second_backend, config(second));
auto lobby = lobby_app.join("lobby");
auto kitchen = kitchen_app.join("kitchen");
// What each app's backend was asked for, once both rooms have met the other peer.
const auto report = [&] {
    std::cout << "the lobby's relays: " << relays_of(first_backend) << '\n'
              << "the kitchen's relays: " << relays_of(second_backend) << '\n'
              << "the lobby's connection: " << ice_servers_of(first_backend) << " ICE servers\n"
              << "the kitchen's connection: " << ice_servers_of(second_backend)
              << " ICE servers\n";
};
The twin, on Trystero JS
import {getRelaySockets, joinRoom} from 'trystero'
import {RTCPeerConnection} from 'werift'
import {openPage} from '../page.mjs'

const relay = process.env.TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL
const config = {appId: 'webcpp-trystero-differences', rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}
// Two configurations. The second relay is the same local relay under a path, which it accepts as
// it accepts any, and its STUN server one where nothing answers; the first has no ICE server, so
// that the peers meet on this machine alone.
const first = {relayConfig: {urls: [relay]}, rtcConfig: {iceServers: []}}
const second = {
    relayConfig: {urls: [`${relay}/second`]},
    rtcConfig: {iceServers: [{urls: 'stun:127.0.0.1:19'}]},
}
// The other peer, another page: the lobby with the first configuration, then, once this page asks,
// the kitchen with the second.
const other = openPage(async ({joinRoom, RTCPeerConnection, data: {first, second}, next}) => {
    const config = {appId: 'webcpp-trystero-differences', rtcPolyfill: RTCPeerConnection}
    const lobby = joinRoom({...config, ...first}, 'lobby')
    await next()
    const kitchen = joinRoom({...config, ...second}, 'kitchen')
    await next()
    await Promise.all([lobby.leave(), kitchen.leave()])
}, {first, second})
// The configuration whose URLs, and only they, are `urls`, each configuration's read by `urlsOf`.
const which = (urls, urlsOf) => {
    const same = c => JSON.stringify([...urls].sort()) === JSON.stringify([...urlsOf(c)].sort())
    return same(first) ? "the first configuration's" : same(second) ? "the second configuration's" : 'another'
}
// The relays the rooms use: the page's relay sockets, which every room of the page shares.
const relaysOf = () => which(Object.keys(getRelaySockets()), c => c.relayConfig.urls)
// The ICE servers of the connection a room meets a peer on.
const iceUrls = rtcConfig => rtcConfig.iceServers.flatMap(server => [server.urls].flat())
const iceServersOf = (room, peer) =>
    which(iceUrls(room.getPeers()[peer].getConfiguration()), c => iceUrls(c.rtcConfig))
const met = room => new Promise(joined => (room.onPeerJoin = joined))

// tag::example[]
// A configuration is a room's: each room is joined with its own.
const lobby = joinRoom({...config, ...first}, 'lobby')
const lobbyPeer = await met(lobby)
// The kitchen, joined with the second configuration once the lobby has met the other peer.
other.post('kitchen')
const kitchen = joinRoom({...config, ...second}, 'kitchen')
const kitchenPeer = await met(kitchen)
console.log(`the lobby's relays: ${relaysOf()}`)
console.log(`the kitchen's relays: ${relaysOf()}`)
console.log(`the lobby's connection: ${iceServersOf(lobby, lobbyPeer)} ICE servers`)
console.log(`the kitchen's connection: ${iceServersOf(kitchen, kitchenPeer)} ICE servers`)
// end::example[]
other.post('leave')
await Promise.all([lobby.leave(), kitchen.leave(), other.done])
Trystero JS prints
the lobby's relays: the first configuration's
the kitchen's relays: the first configuration's
the lobby's connection: the first configuration's ICE servers
the kitchen's connection: the first configuration's ICE servers
trystero prints
the lobby's relays: the first configuration's
the kitchen's relays: the second configuration's
the lobby's connection: the first configuration's ICE servers
the kitchen's connection: the second configuration's ICE servers

Relay sockets

Trystero JS

A page opens one WebSocket per relay, which every room of the page shares, its topics batched on it; getRelaySockets returns them.

trystero

Each room opens its own. The program counts the WebSockets its app asks of the backend, since a room hands out none.

Why

Not part of the decision that shares connections between rooms; peers see no difference. The rooms of an app may share their relays’ sockets in a later change.

trystero::app app(io.get_executor(), backend,
                  {.app_id = "webcpp-trystero-differences", .relay_urls = {relay}});
auto lobby = app.join("lobby");
auto kitchen = app.join("kitchen");
// Once both rooms have started, which they do on the executor.
asio::post(io, [&] {
    std::cout << "the WebSockets the two rooms opened to their one relay: "
              << backend.websockets() << '\n';
    lobby->async_leave([](boost::system::error_code) {});
    kitchen->async_leave([](boost::system::error_code) {});
});
The twin, on Trystero JS
import {getRelaySockets, joinRoom} from 'trystero'

const config = {appId: 'webcpp-trystero-differences', relayConfig: {urls: [process.env.TRYSTERO_RELAY_URL]}}
// tag::example[]
const lobby = joinRoom(config, 'lobby')
const kitchen = joinRoom(config, 'kitchen')
const sockets = Object.values(getRelaySockets())
console.log(`the WebSockets the two rooms opened to their one relay: ${sockets.length}`)
// end::example[]
await Promise.all([lobby.leave(), kitchen.leave()])

the WebSockets the two rooms opened to their one relay: 1
trystero prints
the WebSockets the two rooms opened to their one relay: 2

on_peer_join does not replay the joined peers

Trystero JS

A newly set onPeerJoin is called at once with each peer already joined.

trystero

A room reports a join from its executor, after the call to join has returned, to the handler set then, so a handler set right after join sees every join; peers() lists the joined peers for a handler set later.

Why

A join is an event, reported once; the peers joined are the room’s state, which peers() reads.

int late_calls = 0;
room.on_peer_join([&](std::string_view) {
    std::cout << "the handler set before the join: called\n";
    // Once the join is reported, another handler replaces this one.
    asio::post(io, [&] {
        room.on_peer_join([&late_calls](std::string_view) { ++late_calls; });
        asio::post(io, [&] {
            std::cout << "the handler set after the join: "
                      << (late_calls == 0 ? "not called" : "called") << '\n'
                      << "peers: " << room.peers().size() << '\n';
            leave();
        });
    });
});

// tag::example[]

A send to a peer that has not joined fails

Trystero JS

The send warns on the console, "no peer with id …​ found", and resolves.

trystero

async_send completes with error::no_such_peer. With several targets, the send still goes to the others, and completes with the first failure.

Why

An operation that fails says so with its error code, which a program can act on, and a console’s warning is not.

auto greeting = room.make_action<std::string>("greeting");

                                  << (ec ? "failed: " + ec.message() : "succeeded") << '\n';
                        room.async_leave([](boost::system::error_code) {});
                    });
